Sir Hugh, persuade me not. I will make a Star Chamber matter of it. If / he were twenty Sir John Falstaffs, he shall not abuse Robert Shallow, / esquire.
Sir Hugh, don't try to talk me out of it. I will take this to the Star Chamber. Even if he were twenty Sir John Falstaffs, he will not insult Robert Shallow, esquire.
In the county of Gloucester, Justice of Peace and Coram.
In the county of Gloucester, Justice of the Peace and Coram.
Yes, cousin Slender, and Custalorum too.
Ay, and Ratolorum too; and a gentleman born, Master Parson, who writes / himself "Armigero" in any bill, warrant, quittance, or / obligation—"Armigero."
Yes, and Ratolorum as well; and a gentleman by birth, Master Parson, who signs himself "Armigero", meaning entitled to a coat of arms, on any bill, warrant, receipt or bond. "Armigero."
Ay, that I do, and have done any time these three hundred years.
Yes, I do, and have done for the last three hundred years.
All his successors, gone before him hath done't; and all his ancestors / that come after him may. They may give the dozen white luces in their / coat.
All his successors who went before him have done it, and all his ancestors who come after him may. They can show the dozen white luces, the pike fish, on their coat of arms.
The dozen white louses do become an old coat well. It agrees well, / passant. It is a familiar beast to man, and signifies love.
The dozen white lice suit an old coat well. It fits nicely, as they say in heraldry. The louse is a beast very familiar to man, and it stands for love.
The luce is the fresh fish. The salt fish is an old coat.
The luce is the fresh fish. The salt fish is an old coat.
I can add it to my own arms, cousin.
You can, by marrying into it.
It is marring indeed, if he quarter it.
It will be marring indeed, if he quarters it.

Yes, py'r Lady. If he has a quarter of your coat, there is but three / skirts for yourself, in my simple conjectures. But that is all one. If / Sir John Falstaff have committed disparagements unto you, I am of the / Church, and will be glad to do my benevolence to make atonements and / compremises between you.

Yes, by our Lady. If he takes a quarter of your coat, there are only three skirts left for you, in my simple opinion. But never mind that. If Sir John Falstaff has wronged you, I am a man of the Church, and I will gladly do my good office to make peace and a settlement between you.
The Council shall hear it; it is a riot.
The King's Council shall hear about it; it is a riot.
It is not meet the Council hear a riot. There is no fear of Got in a / riot. The Council, look you, shall desire to hear the fear of Got, and / not to hear a riot. Take your vizaments in that.
It is not fitting for the Council to hear a riot. There is no fear of God in a riot. The Council, you see, will want to hear the fear of God, not a riot. Take that into your considerations.
Ha! O' my life, if I were young again, the sword should end it.
Ha! On my life, if I were young again, the sword would settle it.

It is petter that friends is the sword, and end it; and there is also / another device in my prain, which peradventure prings goot discretions / with it. There is Anne Page, which is daughter to Master George Page, / which is pretty virginity.

It is better to let friends be the sword and settle it. And I have another plan in my head that may bring some good sense with it. There is Anne Page, daughter of Master George Page, who is a pretty young maiden.
Mistress Anne Page? She has brown hair, and speaks small like a woman?
Mistress Anne Page? She has brown hair and speaks softly, like a woman?

It is that fery person for all the 'orld, as just as you will desire, / and seven hundred pounds of moneys, and gold, and silver, is her / grandsire upon his death's-bed—Got deliver to a joyful / resurrections!—give, when she is able to overtake seventeen years old. / It were a goot motion if we leave our pribbles and prabbles, and desire / a marriage between Master Abraham and Mistress Anne Page.

That is the very person, exactly as you could wish. And her grandfather on his deathbed (God bring him to a joyful resurrection!) left her seven hundred pounds in money, gold and silver, to be hers when she reaches seventeen. It would be a good idea if we gave up our petty squabbles and arranged a marriage between Master Abraham and Mistress Anne Page.
Did her grandsire leave her seven hundred pound?
Did her grandfather leave her seven hundred pounds?
Ay, and her father is make her a petter penny.
Yes, and her father will give her a better sum still.
I know the young gentlewoman; she has good gifts.
I know the young lady; she has good qualities.
Seven hundred pounds, and possibilities, is goot gifts.
Seven hundred pounds, and more to come, are good qualities.
Well, let us see honest Master Page. Is Falstaff there?
Well, let's go and see honest Master Page. Is Falstaff there?

Shall I tell you a lie? I do despise a liar as I do despise one that is / false, or as I despise one that is not true. The knight Sir John is / there, and I beseech you be ruled by your well-willers. I will peat the / door for Master Page.

Shall I tell you a lie? I hate a liar as much as I hate someone who is false, or someone who is not true. The knight Sir John is there, and I beg you to listen to those who wish you well. I will knock at Master Page's door.
What, ho! Got pless your house here!
Hello there! God bless this house!
Here is Got's plessing, and your friend, and Justice Shallow, and here / young Master Slender, that peradventures shall tell you another tale, / if matters grow to your likings.
God's blessing is here, and your friend, and Justice Shallow, and young Master Slender, who may have another story to tell you, if things go the way you like.
I am glad to see your worships well. I thank you for my venison, Master / Shallow.
I am glad to see your worships well. Thank you for the venison, Master Shallow.

Master Page, I am glad to see you, much good do it your good heart! I / wished your venison better; it was ill killed. How doth good Mistress / Page? And I thank you always with my heart, la, with my heart.

Master Page, I am glad to see you; may it do your kind heart good! I wish the venison had been better; it was badly killed. How is good Mistress Page? I always thank you with all my heart, truly, with all my heart.
Sir, I thank you; by yea and no, I do.
Thank you, sir; yes indeed, I do.
I am glad to see you, good Master Slender.
I am glad to see you, good Master Slender.
How does your fallow greyhound, sir? I heard say he was outrun on / Cotsall.
How is your fawn-coloured greyhound, sir? I heard he was beaten in the race on the Cotswolds.
It could not be judged, sir.
The result could not be settled, sir.
You'll not confess, you'll not confess.
You won't admit it, you won't admit it.
That he will not. 'Tis your fault; 'tis your fault. 'Tis a good dog.
No, he won't. It's your dog's fault, your dog's fault. It's a good dog.
Sir, he's a good dog, and a fair dog, can there be more said? He is / good, and fair. Is Sir John Falstaff here?
Sir, he's a good dog and a handsome dog; what more can you say? He's good and handsome. Is Sir John Falstaff here?
Sir, he is within; and I would I could do a good office between you.
Sir, he is inside, and I wish I could make peace between you.
It is spoke as a Christians ought to speak.
That is spoken as a Christian ought to speak.
He hath wronged me, Master Page.
He has wronged me, Master Page.
Sir, he doth in some sort confess it.
Sir, he more or less admits it.
If it be confessed, it is not redressed. Is not that so, Master Page? / He hath wronged me, indeed he hath, at a word, he hath. Believe me. / Robert Shallow, esquire, saith he is wronged.
Admitting it is not making amends. Isn't that right, Master Page? He has wronged me, he really has, in a word, he has. Believe me. Robert Shallow, esquire, says he has been wronged.
Now, Master Shallow, you'll complain of me to the King?
Well, Master Shallow, are you going to complain about me to the King?
Knight, you have beaten my men, killed my deer, and broke open my / lodge.
Knight, you have beaten my servants, killed my deer and broken into my hunting lodge.
But not kissed your keeper's daughter!
But I didn't kiss your gamekeeper's daughter!
Tut, a pin! This shall be answered.
Nonsense! You will answer for this.
I will answer it straight: I have done all this. That is now answered.
I will answer right now: I did all of it. There, that's answered.
The Council will hear of this.
'Twere better for you if it were known in counsel: you'll be laughed / at.
It would be better for you if it were kept quiet: you'll be laughed at.
Pauca verba, Sir John; goot worts.
Few words, Sir John; good words.
Good worts? Good cabbage!—Slender, I broke your head. What matter have / you against me?
Good worts? Good cabbages! Slender, I cracked your head. What complaint do you have against me?

Marry, sir, I have matter in my head against you, and against your / cony-catching rascals, Bardolph, Nym, and Pistol. They carried me to / the tavern and made me drunk, and afterwards picked my pocket.
Well, sir, I have a complaint in my head against you, and against your swindling rogues, Bardolph, Nym and Pistol. They took me to the tavern, got me drunk and then picked my pocket.
Slice, I say! Pauca, pauca, slice, that's my humour.
Cut him up, I say! Few words, few words; cut him, that's my mood.
Where's Simple, my man? Can you tell, cousin?
Where's Simple, my servant? Do you know, cousin?

Peace, I pray you. Now let us understand; there is three umpires in / this matter, as I understand: that is, Master Page, fidelicet Master / Page; and there is myself, fidelicet myself; and the three party is, / lastly and finally, mine host of the Garter.

Quiet, please. Now let us understand this. There are three umpires in this matter, as I understand it: that is, Master Page, namely Master Page; and myself, namely myself; and the third party is, lastly and finally, the landlord of the Garter Inn.
We three to hear it and end it between them.
We three will hear the case and settle it between them.
Fery goot. I will make a prief of it in my notebook, and we will / afterwards 'ork upon the cause with as great discreetly as we can.
Very good. I will make a note of it in my notebook, and afterwards we will work on the case as carefully as we can.
The tevil and his tam! What phrase is this, "He hears with ear"? Why, / it is affectations.
The devil and his mother! What way of speaking is that, "He hears with ear"? Why, it is pure affectation.
Pistol, did you pick Master Slender's purse?
Pistol, did you pick Master Slender's purse?

Ay, by these gloves, did he, or I would I might never come in mine own / great chamber again else! Of seven groats in mill-sixpences, and two / Edward shovel-boards that cost me two shilling and two pence a-piece of / Yed Miller, by these gloves.

Yes, by these gloves he did, or may I never set foot in my own great hall again! Seven groats in milled sixpences, and two Edward shovel-board shillings that cost me two shillings and twopence each from Ed Miller, by these gloves.
No, it is false, if it is a pick-purse.
No, it is false, if he is a pickpocket.
Ha, thou mountain-foreigner!—Sir John and master mine, / I combat challenge of this latten bilbo.— / Word of denial in thy labras here! / Word of denial! Froth and scum, thou liest.
Ha, you foreigner from the mountains! Sir John, my master, I challenge this tin-sword weakling to a fight. I throw the denial back in your lips! I deny it! You scum and froth, you lie.
[Points at Nym] By these gloves, then, 'twas he.
By these gloves, then, it was him.
Be avised, sir, and pass good humours. I will say "marry trap with / you", if you run the nuthook's humour on me. That is the very note of / it.
Be careful, sir, and keep your temper. I will say "go hang yourself" if you try to play the constable with me. That's how it stands.
By this hat, then, he in the red face had it. For though I cannot / remember what I did when you made me drunk, yet I am not altogether an / ass.
By this hat, then, the one with the red face took it. Though I can't remember what I did when you got me drunk, I am not a complete fool.
What say you, Scarlet and John?
What do you say, Scarlet and John?
Why, sir, for my part, I say the gentleman had drunk himself out of his / five sentences.
Well, sir, for my part, I say the gentleman had drunk himself out of his five sentences.
It is his "five senses". Fie, what the ignorance is!
It is "five senses". Shame, what ignorance!
And being fap, sir, was, as they say, cashiered; and so conclusions / passed the careers.
And being drunk, sir, he was, as they say, robbed of his cash; and so things went past their limit.

Ay, you spake in Latin then too; but 'tis no matter. I'll ne'er be / drunk whilst I live again, but in honest, civil, godly company, for / this trick. If I be drunk, I'll be drunk with those that have the fear / of God, and not with drunken knaves.

Yes, and you talked Latin then too; but never mind. I'll never get drunk again as long as I live, except in honest, civil, godly company, after this trick. If I get drunk, I'll get drunk with people who fear God, not with drunken rogues.
So Got 'udge me, that is a virtuous mind.
God judge me, that is a virtuous attitude.
You hear all these matters denied, gentlemen; you hear it.
You hear all these charges denied, gentlemen; you hear it.
Nay, daughter, carry the wine in, we'll drink within.
No, daughter, take the wine inside; we'll drink in there.
O heaven, this is Mistress Anne Page.
Oh heaven, this is Mistress Anne Page.
Mistress Ford, by my troth, you are very well met. By your leave, good / mistress.
Mistress Ford, on my word, I am very glad to meet you. With your permission, good lady.
Wife, bid these gentlemen welcome. Come, we have a hot venison pasty to / dinner. Come, gentlemen, I hope we shall drink down all unkindness.
Wife, welcome these gentlemen. Come, we have a hot venison pie for dinner. Come, gentlemen, I hope we will drink away all bad feeling.
I had rather than forty shillings I had my book of Songs and Sonnets / here.
I would give forty shillings to have my book of Songs and Sonnets here.
How now, Simple, where have you been? I must wait on myself, must I? / You have not the Book of Riddles about you, have you?
Well, Simple, where have you been? I have to wait on myself, do I? You haven't got the Book of Riddles with you, have you?
Book of Riddles? Why, did you not lend it to Alice Shortcake upon / Allhallowmas last, a fortnight afore Michaelmas?
The Book of Riddles? Why, didn't you lend it to Alice Shortcake last All Saints' Day, two weeks before Michaelmas?
Come, coz; come, coz, we stay for you. A word with you, coz. Marry, / this, coz: there is, as 'twere, a tender, a kind of tender, made afar / off by Sir Hugh here. Do you understand me?

Come, cousin, come, cousin, we're waiting for you. A word with you, cousin. It's this, cousin: there is, so to speak, an offer, a kind of offer, made indirectly by Sir Hugh here. Do you understand me?
Ay, sir, you shall find me reasonable. If it be so, I shall do that / that is reason.
Yes, sir, you will find me reasonable. If that is so, I will do what is reasonable.
Give ear to his motions, Master Slender. I will description the matter / to you, if you be capacity of it.
Listen to his proposal, Master Slender. I will describe the matter to you, if you are capable of understanding it.
Nay, I will do as my cousin Shallow says. I pray you pardon me, he's a / Justice of Peace in his country, simple though I stand here.
No, I will do what my cousin Shallow says. Excuse me, he's a Justice of the Peace in his county, humble as I may look standing here.
But that is not the question. The question is concerning your marriage.
But that is not the question. The question concerns your marriage.
Marry, is it; the very point of it—to Mistress Anne Page.
Indeed it is, the very point of it: to Mistress Anne Page.
Why, if it be so, I will marry her upon any reasonable demands.
Well, if that's it, I will marry her on any reasonable terms.

But can you affection the 'oman? Let us command to know that of your / mouth, or of your lips; for divers philosophers hold that the lips is / parcel of the mouth. Therefore, precisely, can you carry your good will / to the maid?
But can you love the woman? Let us hear that from your mouth, or from your lips; for many philosophers hold that the lips are part of the mouth. So, exactly, can you give your affection to the girl?
Cousin Abraham Slender, can you love her?
Cousin Abraham Slender, can you love her?
I hope, sir, I will do as it shall become one that would do reason.
I hope, sir, I will behave as someone who wants to be reasonable should.
Nay, Got's lords and his ladies! You must speak possitable, if you can / carry her your desires towards her.
No, by God's lords and ladies! You must say positively whether you can give her your desire.
That you must. Will you, upon good dowry, marry her?
You must. Will you marry her, with a good dowry?
I will do a greater thing than that, upon your request, cousin, in any / reason.
I will do a greater thing than that, if you ask me, cousin, within reason.
Nay, conceive me, conceive me, sweet coz. What I do is to pleasure you, / coz. Can you love the maid?
No, understand me, understand me, dear cousin. What I do is to please you, cousin. Can you love the girl?

I will marry her, sir, at your request. But if there be no great love / in the beginning, yet heaven may decrease it upon better acquaintance, / when we are married and have more occasion to know one another. I hope / upon familiarity will grow more contempt. But if you say "Marry her," I / will marry her. That I am freely dissolved, and dissolutely.

I will marry her, sir, since you ask. And if there isn't much love at the beginning, heaven may decrease it when we know each other better, once we are married and have more chance to get acquainted. I hope that familiarity will breed more contempt. But if you say "Marry her," I will marry her. On that I am freely dissolved, and dissolutely.
It is a fery discretion answer, save the fall is in the 'ord / "dissolutely." The 'ort is, according to our meaning, "resolutely." His / meaning is good.
It is a very sensible answer, except for the slip in the word "dissolutely". The word, as we mean it, is "resolutely". His meaning is good.
Ay, I think my cousin meant well.
Yes, I think my cousin meant well.
Ay, or else I would I might be hanged, la!
Yes, or else may I be hanged, I swear!
Here comes fair Mistress Anne.—Would I were young for your sake, / Mistress Anne.
Here comes lovely Mistress Anne. I wish I were young for your sake, Mistress Anne.
The dinner is on the table, my father desires your worships' company.
Dinner is on the table, and my father would like your worships to join him.
I will wait on him, fair Mistress Anne.
I will join him, lovely Mistress Anne.
'Od's plessed will! I will not be absence at the grace.
By God's blessed will! I won't miss grace.
Will't please your worship to come in, sir?
Will you please come in, sir?
No, I thank you, forsooth, heartily; I am very well.
No, thank you, truly, with all my heart; I am very comfortable here.
Dinner is waiting for you, sir.
I am not a-hungry, I thank you, forsooth. [To Simple] Go, sirrah, / for all you are my man, go wait upon my cousin Shallow.
I'm not hungry, thank you, truly. Go, fellow, even if you are my servant, go and wait on my cousin Shallow.
A Justice of Peace sometime may be beholding to his friend for a man. I / keep but three men and a boy yet, till my mother be dead. But what / though? Yet I live like a poor gentleman born.
A Justice of the Peace may sometimes have to borrow a servant from his friend. I keep only three men and a boy for now, until my mother dies. But what of it? I still live like a poor gentleman born.
I may not go in without your worship. They will not sit till you come.
I'm not allowed to go in without your worship. They won't sit down until you come.
I' faith, I'll eat nothing. I thank you as much as though I did.
Honestly, I'll eat nothing. I thank you as much as if I did.
I pray you, sir, walk in.

I had rather walk here, I thank you. I bruised my shin th' other day / with playing at sword and dagger with a master of fence—three veneys / for a dish of stewed prunes—and, by my troth, I cannot abide the smell / of hot meat since. Why do your dogs bark so? Be there bears i' the / town?

I'd rather walk out here, thank you. I bruised my shin the other day fencing with sword and dagger against a fencing master, three bouts for a dish of stewed prunes, and, on my word, I haven't been able to stand the smell of hot meat since. Why are your dogs barking like that? Are there bears in town?
I think there are, sir; I heard them talked of.
I think there are, sir; I heard people talking about them.
I love the sport well, but I shall as soon quarrel at it as any man in / England. You are afraid, if you see the bear loose, are you not?
I love the sport, but I'm as quick to object to it as any man in England. You are afraid when you see the bear loose, aren't you?

That's meat and drink to me now. I have seen Sackerson loose twenty / times, and have taken him by the chain. But, I warrant you, the women / have so cried and shrieked at it that it passed. But women, indeed, / cannot abide 'em; they are very ill-favoured rough things.

That's meat and drink to me. I've seen Sackerson, the famous bear, loose twenty times and grabbed him by the chain. But I promise you, the women screamed and shrieked so much it was beyond belief. Women really can't stand them; they're very ugly, rough things.
Come, gentle Master Slender, come. We stay for you.
Come, gentle Master Slender, come. We're waiting for you.
I'll eat nothing, I thank you, sir.
I'll eat nothing, thank you, sir.
By cock and pie, you shall not choose, sir! Come, come.
By God and the holy book, you have no choice, sir! Come, come.
Nay, pray you lead the way.
Mistress Anne, yourself shall go first.
Not I, sir; pray you keep on.
Not me, sir; please, go on.
Truly, I will not go first; truly, la! I will not do you that wrong.
Honestly, I won't go first; honestly I won't! I won't do you that wrong.
I'll rather be unmannerly than troublesome. You do yourself wrong, / indeed, la!
I'd rather be rude than a nuisance. You do yourself wrong, really, you do!

Go your ways, and ask of Doctor Caius' house which is the way. And / there dwells one Mistress Quickly, which is in the manner of his nurse, / or his dry nurse, or his cook, or his laundry, his washer and his / wringer.
Off you go, and ask the way to Doctor Caius's house. A Mistress Quickly lives there, who is a sort of nurse to him, or his dry nurse, or his cook, or his laundress, his washer and his wringer.

Nay, it is petter yet. Give her this letter. For it is a 'oman that / altogether's acquaintance with Mistress Anne Page; and the letter is to / desire and require her to solicit your master's desires to Mistress / Anne Page. I pray you be gone. I will make an end of my dinner; there's / pippins and cheese to come.

No, there's something better yet. Give her this letter. She is a woman who is very well acquainted with Mistress Anne Page, and the letter asks and requires her to press your master's suit with Mistress Anne Page. Please go. I will finish my dinner; there are apples and cheese still to come.
What says my bully rook? Speak scholarly and wisely.
What does my fine fellow say? Speak learnedly and wisely.
Truly, mine host, I must turn away some of my followers.
Honestly, landlord, I have to dismiss some of my followers.
Discard, bully Hercules; cashier. Let them wag; trot, trot.
Get rid of them, my mighty Hercules; sack them. Let them go; off they trot.
I sit at ten pounds a week.
I'm paying ten pounds a week here.
Thou'rt an emperor—Caesar, Keiser, and Pheazar. I will entertain / Bardolph. He shall draw, he shall tap. Said I well, bully Hector?
You're an emperor, a Caesar, a Kaiser and a Vizier. I will take on Bardolph. He can draw beer and tap the barrels. Well said, my brave Hector?
I have spoke, let him follow.—Let me see thee froth and lime. I am at a / word, follow.
I have spoken; let him follow me. (To Bardolph) Let me see you froth the beer and doctor the wine. I am a man of my word; follow me.
Bardolph, follow him. A tapster is a good trade. An old cloak makes a / new jerkin; a withered servingman a fresh tapster. Go, adieu.
Bardolph, follow him. Tapster is a good trade. An old cloak makes a new jacket, and a worn-out servant makes a fresh tapster. Go, goodbye.
It is a life that I have desired. I will thrive.
It is the life I have always wanted. I will do well.
O base Hungarian wight, wilt thou the spigot wield?
You low beggarly fellow, will you work the tap?
He was gotten in drink. Is not the humour conceited?
He was conceived while his parents were drunk. Isn't that a clever idea?
I am glad I am so acquit of this tinderbox. His thefts were too open. / His filching was like an unskilful singer, he kept not time.
I am glad to be rid of this tinderbox. His thefts were too obvious. His stealing was like a clumsy singer: he never kept time.
The good humour is to steal at a minute's rest.
The best way is to steal in the space of a moment's rest.
"Convey," the wise it call. "Steal?" Foh! A fico for the phrase!
"Convey" is what wise men call it. "Steal"? Pah! A fig for the word!
Well, sirs, I am almost out at heels.
Well, gentlemen, I have almost worn through my shoes.
There is no remedy, I must cony-catch, I must shift.
There's no help for it; I must swindle, I must live by my wits.
Which of you know Ford of this town?
Which of you knows Ford of this town?
I ken the wight, he is of substance good.
I know the man; he is well off.
My honest lads, I will tell you what I am about.
My honest lads, I will tell you what I am about.

No quips now, Pistol. Indeed, I am in the waist two yards about, but I / am now about no waste; I am about thrift. Briefly, I do mean to make / love to Ford's wife. I spy entertainment in her. She discourses, she / carves, she gives the leer of invitation. I can construe the action of / her familiar style; and the hardest voice of her behaviour, to be / Englished rightly, is "I am Sir John Falstaff's."

No jokes now, Pistol. Yes, I am two yards about the waist, but I am not about waste now; I am about thrift. In short, I intend to make love to Ford's wife. I see a welcome in her. She chats, she is gracious, she gives me inviting looks. I can interpret the meaning of her friendly manner, and the strictest reading of her behaviour, put into plain English, is "I belong to Sir John Falstaff."
He hath studied her will and translated her will—out of honesty into / English.
He has studied what she wants and translated it, out of honesty into English.
The anchor is deep. Will that humour pass?
The anchor is deep. Will that idea work?
Now, the report goes she has all the rule of her husband's purse. He / hath a legion of angels.
Now, the rumour is that she has full control of her husband's money. He has a legion of gold angels.
As many devils entertain, and "To her, boy," say I.
Then take on as many devils, and "Go for her, boy," I say.
The humour rises; it is good. Humour me the angels.
The mood rises; it's good. Get me those angels.

I have writ me here a letter to her; and here another to Page's wife, / who even now gave me good eyes too, examined my parts with most / judicious oeillades. Sometimes the beam of her view gilded my foot, / sometimes my portly belly.

I have written a letter to her here, and here is another to Page's wife, who gave me the eye just now as well and looked me over with very knowing glances. Sometimes the beam of her look gilded my foot, sometimes my stately belly.
Then did the sun on dunghill shine.
Then the sun shone on a dunghill.
I thank thee for that humour.

O, she did so course o'er my exteriors with such a greedy intention / that the appetite of her eye did seem to scorch me up like a / burning-glass. Here's another letter to her. She bears the purse too; / she is a region in Guiana, all gold and bounty. I will be cheaters to / them both, and they shall be exchequers to me; they shall be my East / and West Indies, and I will trade to them both. Go, bear thou this / letter to Mistress Page;—and thou this to Mistress Ford. We will / thrive, lads, we will thrive.

Oh, she ran her eyes over my outside with such greedy attention that the hunger in her look seemed to burn me up like a magnifying glass. Here's another letter to her. She controls the purse too; she is like a region of Guiana, all gold and riches. I will be the swindler of both of them, and they will be my treasuries; they will be my East and West Indies, and I will trade with both. Go, take this letter to Mistress Page, and you take this one to Mistress Ford. We will do well, lads, we will do well.
Shall I Sir Pandarus of Troy become, / And by my side wear steel? Then Lucifer take all!
Shall I become a pimp like Pandarus of Troy, with a sword at my side? Then the devil take everything!
I will run no base humour. Here, take the humour-letter. I will keep / the 'haviour of reputation.
I won't do anything so low. Here, take back your letter. I will keep my good name.

[To Robin] Hold, sirrah, bear you these letters tightly; / Sail like my pinnace to these golden shores.— / Rogues, hence, avaunt! Vanish like hailstones, go! / Trudge, plod away o' th' hoof, seek shelter, pack! / Falstaff will learn the humour of this age: / French thrift, you rogues—myself and skirted page.

(To Robin) Here, boy, carry these letters carefully. Sail like my little ship to these golden shores. Rogues, away, be gone! Vanish like hailstones, go! Trudge off on foot, find your own shelter, clear out! Falstaff will follow the fashion of the times: French thrift, you rogues, myself and one page in a short coat.
Let vultures gripe thy guts! For gourd and fullam holds, / And high and low beguile the rich and poor. / Tester I'll have in pouch when thou shalt lack, / Base Phrygian Turk!
May vultures tear your guts! Loaded dice will serve us, and cheating will fool both rich and poor. I'll have sixpence in my pocket when you have nothing, you low heathen!
I have operations in my head which be humours of revenge.
I have plans in my head that are schemes of revenge.
By the sky and its stars!
With both the humours, I. / I will discuss the humour of this love to Ford.
With both. I will reveal this love affair to Ford.
And I to Page shall eke unfold / How Falstaff, varlet vile, / His dove will prove, his gold will hold, / And his soft couch defile.
And I will also tell Page how Falstaff, the vile rascal, means to test his wife, take his gold and dirty his marriage bed.
My humour shall not cool. I will incense Ford to deal with poison, I / will possess him with yellowness, for the revolt of mine is dangerous. / That is my true humour.
My anger won't cool. I will stir Ford up to use poison; I will fill him with jealousy, because my rebellion is dangerous. That is my true mood.
Thou art the Mars of malcontents. I second thee. Troop on.
You are the god of war among malcontents. I'm with you. March on.

I pray thee go to the casement, and see if you can see my master, / Master Doctor Caius, coming. If he do, i' faith, and find anybody in / the house, here will be an old abusing of God's patience and the King's / English.
Please go to the window and see if you can see my master, Doctor Caius, coming. If he does come and finds anyone in the house, there will be a fine old abuse of God's patience and the King's English.
Go; and we'll have a posset for't soon at night, in faith, at the / latter end of a sea-coal fire.
Go, and we'll have a hot spiced drink for it later tonight, honestly, when the coal fire is dying down.

An honest, willing, kind fellow, as ever servant shall come in house / withal; and, I warrant you, no tell-tale nor no breed-bate. His worst / fault is that he is given to prayer; he is something peevish that way, / but nobody but has his fault. But let that pass. Peter Simple you say / your name is?

An honest, willing, kind fellow, as good a servant as ever came into a house, and I promise you, no tell-tale and no troublemaker. His worst fault is that he is too fond of prayer; he's a bit silly that way, but everyone has a fault. But never mind that. Your name is Peter Simple, you say?
Ay, for fault of a better.
Yes, for lack of a better one.
And Master Slender is your master?
Does he not wear a great round beard, like a glover's paring-knife?
Doesn't he wear a big round beard, like a glove-maker's curved knife?
No, forsooth, he hath but a little wee face, with a little yellow / beard, a Cain-coloured beard.
No, truly, he has just a tiny little face, with a little yellow beard, a reddish-yellow beard like Cain's.
A softly-sprighted man, is he not?
Ay, forsooth. But he is as tall a man of his hands as any is between / this and his head. He hath fought with a warrener.
Yes, truly. But he is as brave a fighter as anyone between here and there. He once fought with a gamekeeper.
How say you? O, I should remember him. Does he not hold up his head, as / it were, and strut in his gait?
What's that? Oh, I should remember him. Doesn't he hold his head up high, so to speak, and strut when he walks?
Well, heaven send Anne Page no worse fortune! Tell Master Parson Evans / I will do what I can for your master. Anne is a good girl, and I wish—
Well, heaven send Anne Page no worse luck! Tell Parson Evans I will do what I can for your master. Anne is a good girl, and I wish—
Out, alas! Here comes my master.
Oh no! Here comes my master.
We shall all be shent. Run in here, good young man, go into this / closet. He will not stay long.
We'll all be in trouble. Run in here, good young man, go into this cupboard. He won't stay long.
What, John Rugby! John! What, John, I say! Go, John, go inquire for my / master. I doubt he be not well, that he comes not home.
John Rugby! John! John, I say! Go, John, go and look for my master. I'm afraid he isn't well, since he hasn't come home.
And down, down, adown-a, and so on.
Vat is you sing? I do not like dese toys. Pray you, go and vetch me in / my closet une boîtine verte, a box, a green-a box. Do intend vat I / speak? A green-a box.
What is it you are singing? I don't like these trifles. Please go and fetch me from my cupboard a little green box, a box, a green box. Do you understand what I am saying? A green box.
Ay, forsooth, I'll fetch it you. / [Aside] I am glad he went not in himself. If he had found the young / man, he would have been horn-mad.
Yes, truly, I'll fetch it for you. (Aside) I'm glad he didn't go in himself. If he had found the young man, he would have gone mad with rage.
Fe, fe, fe fe! Ma foi, il fait fort chaud. Je m'en vais à la cour—la / grande affaire.
Phew, phew, phew! My word, it's very hot. I am going to the court, on the great business.
Oui, mette-le au mon pocket. Dépêche, quickly—Vere is dat knave / Rugby?
Yes, put it in my pocket. Hurry, quickly. Where is that rogue Rugby?
You are John Rugby, and you are Jack Rugby. Come, take-a your rapier, / and come after my heel to the court.
You are John Rugby, and you are Jack Rugby. Come, take your rapier and follow at my heels to the court.
'Tis ready, sir, here in the porch.
It's ready, sir, here in the porch.
By my trot, I tarry too long. 'Od's me! Qu'ay j'oublié? Dere is some / simples in my closet dat I vill not for the varld I shall leave behind.
On my word, I'm taking too long. God save me! What have I forgotten? There are some herbs in my cupboard that I wouldn't leave behind for the world.
Ay me, he'll find the young man there, and be mad!
Oh dear, he'll find the young man there and go mad!
O diable, diable! Vat is in my closet? Villainy! Larron! [Pulling / Simple out.] Rugby, my rapier!
Oh devil, devil! What is in my cupboard? Villainy! Thief! Rugby, my rapier!
The young man is an honest man.
The young man is an honest man.
What shall de honest man do in my closet? Dere is no honest man dat / shall come in my closet.
What is an honest man doing in my cupboard? No honest man comes into my cupboard.
I beseech you, be not so phlegmatic. Hear the truth of it. He came of / an errand to me from Parson Hugh.
Please don't be so hot-tempered. Hear the truth of it. He came to me on an errand from Parson Hugh.
Ay, forsooth, to desire her to—
Yes, truly, to ask her to—
You hold your tongue! You, tell your story.
To desire this honest gentlewoman, your maid, to speak a good word to / Mistress Anne Page for my master in the way of marriage.
To ask this honest woman, your servant, to put in a good word for my master with Mistress Anne Page, with a view to marriage.
This is all, indeed, la! But I'll ne'er put my finger in the fire, and / need not.
That's all it is, truly! But I'll never put my finger in the fire when I don't have to.
Sir Hugh send-a you?—Rugby, baille me some paper.—Tarry you a / little-a while.
Sir Hugh sent you? Rugby, give me some paper. You wait here a little while.

[Aside to Simple] I am glad he is so quiet. If he had been throughly / moved, you should have heard him so loud and so melancholy. But / notwithstanding, man, I'll do you your master what good I can; and the / very yea and the no is, the French doctor, my master—I may call him my / master, look you, for I keep his house, and I wash, wring, brew, bake, / scour, dress meat and drink, make the beds, and do all myself—

(Aside to Simple) I'm glad he's so quiet. If he had been thoroughly roused, you would have heard him shout and rage. But all the same, man, I'll do your master what good I can. And the long and short of it is that the French doctor, my master (I can call him my master, you see, because I keep his house, and I wash, wring, brew, bake, scrub, cook and make the drink, make the beds and do it all myself)—
[Aside to Mistress Quickly] 'Tis a great charge to come under one / body's hand.
(Aside to Mistress Quickly) That's a lot of work for one person to handle.

[Aside to Simple] Are you avised o' that? You shall find it a great / charge, and to be up early and down late; but notwithstanding—to tell / you in your ear, I would have no words of it—my master himself is in / love with Mistress Anne Page; but notwithstanding that, I know Anne's / mind. That's neither here nor there.

(Aside to Simple) Have you noticed that? You'd find it's a lot of work, up early and to bed late. But all the same (to whisper it in your ear, and I don't want this talked about) my master himself is in love with Mistress Anne Page. But all the same, I know Anne's mind. That's neither here nor there.

You jack'nape, give-a dis letter to Sir Hugh. By gar, it is a / shallenge. I will cut his troat in de park, and I will teach a scurvy / jackanape priest to meddle or make. You may be gone, it is not good you / tarry here.—By gar, I will cut all his two stones. By gar, he shall not / have a stone to throw at his dog.

You monkey, give this letter to Sir Hugh. By God, it is a challenge. I will cut his throat in the park, and I will teach a lousy monkey of a priest to meddle in my affairs. You can go; it's not good for you to stay here. By God, I will cut off both his balls. By God, he won't have a stone left to throw at his dog.
Alas, he speaks but for his friend.
Oh dear, he's only speaking for his friend.

It is no matter-a ver dat. Do not you tell-a me dat I shall have Anne / Page for myself? By gar, I vill kill de Jack priest; and I have / appointed mine host of de Jarteer to measure our weapon. By gar, I will / myself have Anne Page.

That doesn't matter. Didn't you tell me I would have Anne Page for myself? By God, I will kill that rascal priest; and I have asked the landlord of the Garter to referee our duel. By God, I will have Anne Page myself.
Sir, the maid loves you, and all shall be well. We must give folks / leave to prate. What, the good-year!
Sir, the girl loves you, and all will be well. We have to let people chatter. What the devil!
Rugby, come to the court with me. [To Mistress Quickly] By gar, if I / have not Anne Page, I shall turn your head out of my door.—Follow my / heels, Rugby.
Rugby, come to the court with me. (To Mistress Quickly) By God, if I don't get Anne Page, I will throw you out of my house. Follow at my heels, Rugby.
You shall have An—fool's head of your own. No, I know Anne's mind for / that. Never a woman in Windsor knows more of Anne's mind than I do, nor / can do more than I do with her, I thank heaven.
You'll have Anne—a fool's head of your own, that's what. No, I know Anne's mind on that. No woman in Windsor knows Anne's mind better than I do, or can do more with her than I can, thank heaven.
Who's there, I trow? Come near the house, I pray you.
Who's there, I wonder? Come into the house, please.
How now, good woman? How dost thou?
Hello, good woman! How are you?
The better, that it pleases your good worship to ask.
All the better for your kind worship asking.
What news? How does pretty Mistress Anne?
What news? How is pretty Mistress Anne?
In truth, sir, and she is pretty, and honest, and gentle; and one that / is your friend, I can tell you that by the way, I praise heaven for it.
Truly, sir, she is pretty, and virtuous, and gentle; and she is a friend of yours, I can tell you that in passing, thank heaven.
Shall I do any good, think'st thou? Shall I not lose my suit?
Do you think I'll have any success? Won't I lose my suit?
Troth, sir, all is in His hands above. But notwithstanding, Master / Fenton, I'll be sworn on a book she loves you. Have not your worship a / wart above your eye?
Honestly, sir, it's all in the hands of God above. But all the same, Master Fenton, I'd swear on the Bible she loves you. Doesn't your worship have a wart above your eye?
Yes, marry, have I; what of that?
Yes, I do indeed; what about it?

Well, thereby hangs a tale. Good faith, it is such another Nan! But, I / detest, an honest maid as ever broke bread. We had an hour's talk of / that wart. I shall never laugh but in that maid's company. But, indeed, / she is given too much to allicholy and musing. But for you—well, go to.

Well, there's a story about that. Truly, she's such a girl, our Nan! But, I swear (I mean protest), as virtuous a girl as ever broke bread. We talked about that wart for an hour. I never laugh except when I'm with that girl. But she is really too given to melancholy and daydreaming. But as for you, well, go on.
Well, I shall see her today. Hold, there's money for thee. Let me have / thy voice in my behalf. If thou seest her before me, commend me.
Well, I will see her today. Here, there's some money for you. Speak up for me. If you see her before I do, give her my regards.
Will I? I' faith, that we will! And I will tell your worship more of / the wart the next time we have confidence, and of other wooers.
Will I? Of course I will! And I'll tell your worship more about the wart the next time we have a confidential talk, and about other suitors.
Well, farewell, I am in great haste now.
Well, goodbye; I'm in a great hurry now.
Truly, an honest gentleman—but Anne loves him not, for I know Anne's / mind as well as another does. Out upon 't, what have I forgot?
Truly, an honest gentleman. But Anne doesn't love him, because I know Anne's mind as well as anyone does. Oh dear, what have I forgotten?

What, have I scaped love-letters in the holiday-time of my beauty, and / am I now a subject for them? Let me see. / [Reads] Ask me no reason why I love you, for though Love use Reason / for his precisian, he admits him not for his counsellor. You are not / young, no more am I. Go to, then, there's sympathy. You are merry, so / am I. Ha, ha, then there's more sympathy. You love sack, and so do I. / Would you desire better sympathy? Let it suffice thee, Mistress Page, / at the least, if the love of soldier can suffice, that I love thee. I / will not say, pity me—'tis not a soldier-like phrase—but I say love me. / By me, / Thine own true knight, / By day or night, / Or any kind of light, / With all his might, / For thee to fight, / John Falstaff. / What a Herod of Jewry is this! O wicked, wicked world! One that is / well-nigh worn to pieces with age, to show himself a young gallant! / What an unweighed behaviour hath this Flemish drunkard picked—with the / devil's name!—out of my conversation, that he dares in this manner / assay me? Why, he hath not been thrice in my company! What should I say / to him? I was then frugal of my mirth. Heaven forgive me! Why, I'll / exhibit a bill in the parliament for the putting down of men. How shall / I be revenged on him? For revenged I will be, as sure as his guts are / made of puddings.

What, did I escape love letters in the springtime of my beauty, only to become a target for them now? Let me see. (Reads) "Don't ask me the reason why I love you, for though Love may use Reason as his strict adviser, he never takes him as his counsellor. You are not young, and neither am I. Well then, there's a bond between us. You are merry, and so am I. Ha, ha, there's more of a bond. You love sack, and so do I. Could you want a better bond? Let it be enough for you, Mistress Page, at least if a soldier's love is enough, that I love you. I won't say 'pity me', that is not a soldierly phrase, but I say love me. Signed, your own true knight, by day or night, or any kind of light, with all his might, for you to fight, John Falstaff." What a ranting tyrant this is! Oh wicked, wicked world! A man almost worn to pieces with age, showing off as a young lover! What careless behaviour has this Dutch drunkard picked out of my conversation, in the devil's name, that he dares try me like this? Why, he's barely been in my company three times! What could I have said to him? I was sparing with my jokes then. Heaven forgive me! Why, I'll bring a bill before Parliament to have men abolished. How shall I get my revenge on him? Because revenge I will have, as surely as his guts are made of sausages.
Mistress Page! Trust me, I was going to your house.
Mistress Page! Honestly, I was on my way to your house.
And, trust me, I was coming to you. You look very ill.
And honestly, I was coming to you. You look very unwell.
Nay, I'll ne'er believe that. I have to show to the contrary.
No, I'll never believe that. I have something to show that proves the opposite.
Faith, but you do, in my mind.
Well, you do look it, to my mind.
Well, I do, then. Yet I say I could show you to the contrary. O, / Mistress Page, give me some counsel.
All right, I do, then. But I tell you I could show you the opposite. Oh, Mistress Page, give me some advice.
O woman, if it were not for one trifling respect, I could come to such / honour!
Oh woman, if it weren't for one little consideration, I could rise to such honour!
Hang the trifle, woman; take the honour. What is it? Dispense with / trifles. What is it?
Hang the little consideration, woman; take the honour. What is it? Forget the trifles. What is it?
If I would but go to hell for an eternal moment or so, I could be / knighted.
If I would just go to hell for an eternal moment or so, I could be made a knight.
What? Thou liest! Sir Alice Ford! These knights will hack, and so thou / shouldst not alter the article of thy gentry.
What? You're lying! Sir Alice Ford! These knights are ten a penny, so you shouldn't change your rank as a gentlewoman.

We burn daylight. Here, read, read. Perceive how I might be knighted. I / shall think the worse of fat men as long as I have an eye to make / difference of men's liking. And yet he would not swear; praised women's / modesty; and gave such orderly and well-behaved reproof to all / uncomeliness that I would have sworn his disposition would have gone to / the truth of his words. But they do no more adhere and keep place / together than the Hundredth Psalm to the tune of "Greensleeves." What / tempest, I trow, threw this whale, with so many tuns of oil in his / belly, ashore at Windsor? How shall I be revenged on him? I think the / best way were to entertain him with hope, till the wicked fire of lust / have melted him in his own grease. Did you ever hear the like?

We're wasting time. Here, read it, read it. See how I could be made a knight. I'll think worse of fat men as long as I have eyes to tell men apart. And yet he never swore; he praised women's modesty, and gave such proper, well-mannered criticism of all bad behaviour that I would have sworn his nature matched his words. But they go together no better than the Hundredth Psalm sung to the tune of "Greensleeves". What storm, I wonder, washed this whale, with so many barrels of oil in his belly, ashore at Windsor? How shall I get my revenge on him? I think the best way would be to keep him hoping until the wicked fire of lust has melted him in his own fat. Have you ever heard anything like it?

Letter for letter, but that the name of Page and Ford differs! To thy / great comfort in this mystery of ill opinions, here's the twin brother / of thy letter. But let thine inherit first, for I protest mine never / shall. I warrant he hath a thousand of these letters, writ with blank / space for different names—sure, more, and these are of the second / edition. He will print them, out of doubt; for he cares not what he / puts into the press, when he would put us two. I had rather be a / giantess and lie under Mount Pelion. Well, I will find you twenty / lascivious turtles ere one chaste man.

Letter for letter, except that the names Page and Ford are different! To comfort you in this mystery of our bad reputations, here is the twin brother of your letter. But let yours be the heir, because I swear mine never will. I bet he has a thousand of these letters, written with a blank space for different names; more, surely, and these are the second edition. No doubt he will print them, since he doesn't care what he puts in the press, when he would put the two of us there. I'd rather be a giantess buried under Mount Pelion. Well, I could find you twenty lustful turtledoves before one chaste man.
Why, this is the very same—the very hand, the very words. What doth he / think of us?
Why, this is exactly the same: the same handwriting, the same words. What does he think of us?

Nay, I know not. It makes me almost ready to wrangle with mine own / honesty. I'll entertain myself like one that I am not acquainted / withal; for, sure, unless he know some strain in me that I know not / myself, he would never have boarded me in this fury.

I don't know. It almost makes me ready to argue with my own virtue. I'll treat myself like someone I don't know; because surely, unless he knows some streak in me I don't know myself, he would never have attacked me so boldly.
"Boarding" call you it? I'll be sure to keep him above deck.
"Boarding", you call it? I'll make sure to keep him above deck.

So will I. If he come under my hatches, I'll never to sea again. Let's / be revenged on him. Let's appoint him a meeting, give him a show of / comfort in his suit, and lead him on with a fine-baited delay, till he / hath pawned his horses to mine host of the Garter.

So will I. If he gets below my hatches, I'll never go to sea again. Let's get our revenge on him. Let's arrange a meeting with him, give him a show of encouragement in his courtship, and lead him on with well-baited delays until he has pawned his horses to the landlord of the Garter.
Nay, I will consent to act any villainy against him that may not sully / the chariness of our honesty. O, that my husband saw this letter! It / would give eternal food to his jealousy.
Yes, I will agree to do any mischief against him that won't stain our careful good name. Oh, if my husband saw this letter! It would feed his jealousy for ever.
Why, look where he comes; and my good man too. He's as far from / jealousy as I am from giving him cause, and that, I hope, is an / unmeasurable distance.
Why, look, here he comes, and my good husband too. He is as far from jealousy as I am from giving him cause, and that, I hope, is an immeasurable distance.
Let's consult together against this greasy knight. Come hither.
Let's plan together against this greasy knight. Come over here.
Well, I hope it be not so.
Well, I hope it isn't true.
Hope is a curtal dog in some affairs. / Sir John affects thy wife.
Hope is a dog with its tail cut short in some matters. Sir John is after your wife.
Why, sir, my wife is not young.
Why, sir, my wife is not young.
He woos both high and low, both rich and poor, / Both young and old, one with another, Ford. / He loves the gallimaufry. Ford, perpend.
He woos high and low, rich and poor, young and old, all alike, Ford. He loves a mixed dish. Ford, think about it.
With liver burning hot. / Prevent, or go thou like Sir Actaeon he, / With Ringwood at thy heels. / O, odious is the name!
With a burning hot liver. Stop him, or you'll go like Actaeon, with the hound Ringwood at your heels. Oh, the name is hateful!

The horn, I say. Farewell. / Take heed, have open eye, for thieves do foot by night. / Take heed, ere summer comes, or cuckoo birds do sing.— / Away, Sir Corporal Nym.—Believe it, Page, he speaks sense.
The horn, I say. Goodbye. Be careful, keep your eyes open, for thieves walk at night. Be careful before summer comes and the cuckoo sings. Come away, Corporal Nym. Believe him, Page; he talks sense.
[Aside] I will be patient. I will find out this.
(Aside) I will be patient. I will find out about this.

[To Page] And this is true, I like not the humour of lying. He hath / wronged me in some humours. I should have borne the humoured letter to / her; but I have a sword, and it shall bite upon my necessity. He loves / your wife; there's the short and the long. My name is Corporal Nym. I / speak, and I avouch 'tis true. My name is Nym, and Falstaff loves your / wife. Adieu. I love not the humour of bread and cheese. Adieu.

(To Page) And this is true; I don't like lying. He has wronged me in certain ways. I was supposed to carry his fancy letter to her; but I have a sword, and it will bite when I need it. He loves your wife; that's the long and short of it. My name is Corporal Nym. I say it and I swear it's true. My name is Nym, and Falstaff loves your wife. Goodbye. I don't care for a diet of bread and cheese. Goodbye.
[Aside] "The humour of it," quoth 'a! Here's a fellow frights / English out of his wits.
(Aside) "The humour of it," he says! Here's a fellow who frightens English out of its wits.
[Aside] I never heard such a drawling, affecting rogue.
(Aside) I never heard such a drawling, affected rogue.
(Aside) If I do find it's true, well.
[Aside] I will not believe such a Cataian, though the priest o' the / town commended him for a true man.
(Aside) I won't believe such a scoundrel, even if the town priest vouched for him as an honest man.
(Aside) He was a good, sensible fellow. Well.
Whither go you, George? Hark you.
Where are you going, George? Listen.
How now, sweet Frank, why art thou melancholy?
What's the matter, dear Frank? Why are you gloomy?
I melancholy? I am not melancholy. Get you home, go.
Me, gloomy? I'm not gloomy. Go home, go.
Faith, thou hast some crotchets in thy head now.—Will you go, Mistress / Page?
Really, you have some strange notion in your head now. Shall we go, Mistress Page?
Have with you. You'll come to dinner, George? / [Aside to Mistress Ford] Look who comes yonder. She shall be our / messenger to this paltry knight.
I'm with you. You'll come home to dinner, George? (Aside to Mistress Ford) Look who's coming over there. She will be our messenger to this worthless knight.
[Aside to Mistress Page] Trust me, I thought on her. She'll fit it.
(Aside to Mistress Page) Honestly, I was thinking of her. She'll be just right for it.
You are come to see my daughter Anne?
Have you come to see my daughter Anne?
Ay, forsooth. And, I pray, how does good Mistress Anne?
Yes, truly. And please, how is good Mistress Anne?
Go in with us and see. We'd have an hour's talk with you.
Come in with us and see. We'd like an hour's talk with you.
You heard what this knave told me, did you not?
You heard what this rogue told me, didn't you?
Yes, and you heard what the other told me?
Yes, and you heard what the other one told me?
Do you think there is truth in them?
Do you think there is any truth in them?
Hang 'em, slaves! I do not think the knight would offer it, but these / that accuse him in his intent towards our wives are a yoke of his / discarded men, very rogues, now they be out of service.
Hang them, the wretches! I don't think the knight would try it; and these men who accuse him of designs on our wives are a pair of his sacked servants, real rogues, now that they're out of work.
I like it never the better for that. Does he lie at the Garter?
I don't like it any better for that. Is he staying at the Garter?
Ay, marry, does he. If he should intend this voyage toward my wife, I / would turn her loose to him; and what he gets more of her than sharp / words, let it lie on my head.
Yes, he is. If he were planning this voyage towards my wife, I would let her loose on him; and if he gets anything more from her than sharp words, let the blame fall on my head.
I do not misdoubt my wife, but I would be loath to turn them together. / A man may be too confident. I would have nothing lie on my head. I / cannot be thus satisfied.
I don't doubt my wife, but I wouldn't like to leave them together. A man can be too confident. I wouldn't want anything to fall on my head. I can't be satisfied like this.
Look where my ranting host of the Garter comes. There is either liquor / in his pate or money in his purse when he looks so merrily.—How now, / mine host?
Look, here comes my loud landlord of the Garter. Either there's drink in his head or money in his purse when he looks so cheerful. Hello, landlord!
How now, bully rook? Thou'rt a gentleman.—Cavaliero Justice, I say!
Hello, my fine fellow! You're a gentleman. Sir Justice, come on, I say!
I follow, mine host, I follow.—Good even and twenty, good Master Page. / Master Page, will you go with us? We have sport in hand.
I'm coming, landlord, I'm coming. Good evening twenty times over, good Master Page. Master Page, will you come with us? We have some fun on hand.
Tell him, Cavaliero Justice; tell him, bully rook.
Tell him, Sir Justice; tell him, my fine fellow.
Sir, there is a fray to be fought between Sir Hugh the Welsh priest and / Caius the French doctor.
Sir, there is a duel to be fought between Sir Hugh, the Welsh priest, and Caius, the French doctor.
Good mine host o' the Garter, a word with you.
Good landlord of the Garter, a word with you.
What say'st thou, my bully rook?
What do you say, my fine fellow?

[To Page] Will you go with us to behold it? My merry host hath had / the measuring of their weapons, and, I think, hath appointed them / contrary places; for, believe me, I hear the parson is no jester. Hark, / I will tell you what our sport shall be.

(To Page) Will you come with us to watch it? My merry landlord has been put in charge of their weapons and, I think, has sent them to different places; because, believe me, I hear the parson is no joker. Listen, I'll tell you what our fun will be.
Hast thou no suit against my knight, my guest cavaliero?
You don't have a quarrel with my knight, my noble guest, do you?
None, I protest. But I'll give you a pottle of burnt sack to give me / recourse to him, and tell him my name is Brook, only for a jest.
None, I swear. But I'll give you a half-gallon of hot sack if you get me in to see him and tell him my name is Brook, just as a joke.
My hand, bully. Thou shalt have egress and regress—said I well?—and thy / name shall be Brook. It is a merry knight. Will you go, myn-heers?
Shake on it, my fine fellow. You shall have the run of the place (well said, wasn't it?) and your name shall be Brook. He's a merry knight. Shall we go, gentlemen?
I have heard the Frenchman hath good skill in his rapier.
I've heard the Frenchman is very skilled with the rapier.

Tut, sir, I could have told you more. In these times you stand on / distance—your passes, stoccadoes, and I know not what. 'Tis the heart, / Master Page; 'tis here, 'tis here. I have seen the time, with my long / sword I would have made you four tall fellows skip like rats.

Pooh, sir, I could have told you more. These days you fuss about distance, your passes, your thrusts and I don't know what. It's courage, Master Page; it's here, it's here. There was a time when with my long sword I'd have made four big fellows skip like rats.
Here, boys, here, here! Shall we wag?
Come on, boys, come on! Shall we go?
Have with you. I had rather hear them scold than fight.
I'm with you. I'd rather hear them argue than fight.

Though Page be a secure fool, and stands so firmly on his wife's / frailty, yet I cannot put off my opinion so easily. She was in his / company at Page's house, and what they made there I know not. Well, I / will look further into 't, and I have a disguise to sound Falstaff. If / I find her honest, I lose not my labour. If she be otherwise, 'tis / labour well bestowed.

Page may be an overconfident fool who relies so firmly on his weak wife, but I can't dismiss my suspicion so easily. She was with Falstaff at Page's house, and I don't know what they did there. Well, I will look into it further, and I have a disguise to sound out Falstaff. If I find she is faithful, my effort is not wasted. If she isn't, it's effort well spent.
I will not lend thee a penny.
I won't lend you a penny.
Why then, the world's mine oyster, / Which I with sword will open.
Then the world is my oyster, which I will open with my sword.

Not a penny. I have been content, sir, you should lay my countenance to / pawn; I have grated upon my good friends for three reprieves for you / and your coach-fellow Nym, or else you had looked through the grate / like a gemini of baboons. I am damned in hell for swearing to gentlemen / my friends you were good soldiers and tall fellows. And when Mistress / Bridget lost the handle of her fan, I took 't upon mine honour thou / hadst it not.

Not a penny. I've allowed you to pawn my good name, sir; I've pestered my good friends for three pardons for you and your partner Nym, or else you'd have been staring through prison bars like a pair of baboons. I am damned to hell for swearing to gentlemen, my friends, that you were good soldiers and brave fellows. And when Mistress Bridget lost the handle of her fan, I swore on my honour that you didn't have it.
Didst not thou share? Hadst thou not fifteen pence?
Didn't you get a share? Didn't you get fifteen pence?

Reason, you rogue, reason. Think'st thou I'll endanger my soul gratis? / At a word, hang no more about me, I am no gibbet for you. Go—a short / knife and a throng—to your manor of Pickt-hatch, go. You'll not bear a / letter for me, you rogue? You stand upon your honour! Why, thou / unconfinable baseness, it is as much as I can do to keep the terms of / my honour precise. Ay, ay, I myself sometimes, leaving the fear of God / on the left hand, and hiding mine honour in my necessity, am fain to / shuffle, to hedge, and to lurch; and yet you, rogue, will ensconce your / rags, your cat-a-mountain looks, your red-lattice phrases, and your / bold beating oaths, under the shelter of your honour! You will not do / it! You!

That was only fair, you rogue, only fair. Do you think I'll risk my soul for nothing? In a word, stop hanging around me; I am not your gallows. Go off, with a short knife for cutting purses in a crowd, to your manor in the brothel district, go. You won't carry a letter for me, you rogue? You stand on your honour! Why, you limitless lowlife, it is as much as I can do to keep my own honour exact. Yes, yes, even I, leaving the fear of God on one side and hiding my honour behind my needs, sometimes have to cheat, to dodge and to steal; and yet you, rogue, want to shelter your rags, your wildcat looks, your tavern talk and your loud bullying oaths behind your honour! You won't do it! You!
I do relent. What wouldst thou more of man?
I give in. What more can you ask of a man?
Sir, here's a woman would speak with you.
Sir, there's a woman here who wants to speak to you.
Not so, an't please your worship.
Not a wife, if it please your worship.
I'll be sworn, as my mother was, the first hour I was born.
I swear I'm as much a maid as my mother was the hour I was born.
I do believe the swearer. What with me?
I believe the swearer. What do you want with me?
Shall I vouchsafe your worship a word or two?
May I grant your worship a word or two?
Two thousand, fair woman; and I'll vouchsafe thee the hearing.
Two thousand, fair woman, and I'll grant you a hearing.
There is one Mistress Ford, sir—I pray, come a little nearer this ways. / I myself dwell with Master Doctor Caius.
There is a Mistress Ford, sir (please come a little closer, this way). I myself live with Doctor Caius.
Well, on; Mistress Ford, you say—
Well, go on. Mistress Ford, you say?
Your worship says very true. I pray your worship come a little nearer / this ways.
Your worship is quite right. Please, your worship, come a little closer this way.
I warrant thee, nobody hears. Mine own people, mine own people.
I promise you, nobody can hear. They're my own people, my own people.
Are they so? God bless them, and make them His servants!
Are they? God bless them and make them His servants!
Well, Mistress Ford, what of her?
Well, Mistress Ford, what about her?
Why, sir, she's a good creature. Lord, Lord, your worship's a wanton! / Well, heaven forgive you, and all of us, I pray!
Why, sir, she's a good creature. Lord, Lord, your worship is a naughty one! Well, heaven forgive you, and all of us, I pray!
Mistress Ford, come on, Mistress Ford.

Marry, this is the short and the long of it: you have brought her into / such a canaries as 'tis wonderful. The best courtier of them all, when / the court lay at Windsor, could never have brought her to such a / canary. Yet there has been knights, and lords, and gentlemen, with / their coaches, I warrant you, coach after coach, letter after letter, / gift after gift, smelling so sweetly, all musk, and so rushling, I / warrant you, in silk and gold, and in such alligant terms, and in such / wine and sugar of the best and the fairest, that would have won any / woman's heart; and I warrant you, they could never get an eye-wink of / her. I had myself twenty angels given me this morning, but I defy all / angels in any such sort, as they say, but in the way of honesty. And, I / warrant you, they could never get her so much as sip on a cup with the / proudest of them all. And yet there has been earls—nay, which is more, / pensioners—but, I warrant you, all is one with her.

Well, this is the long and short of it: you have put her in such a flutter, it's amazing. The best courtier of them all, when the court was at Windsor, could never have got her in such a flutter. And yet there have been knights and lords and gentlemen, with their coaches, I promise you, coach after coach, letter after letter, gift after gift, smelling so sweet, all musk, and rustling, I promise you, in silk and gold, with such elegant words, and such wine and sugar of the finest and best, that would have won any woman's heart; and I promise you, they could never get so much as a wink out of her. I had twenty gold angels given me myself this morning, but I scorn angels of that kind, as they say, unless it's honestly. And I promise you, they could never get her to so much as sip from a cup with the proudest of them. And there have been earls; no, what's more, royal guards; but, I promise you, it's all the same to her.
But what says she to me? Be brief, my good she-Mercury.
But what does she say to me? Keep it short, my good female Mercury.
Marry, she hath received your letter, for the which she thanks you a / thousand times; and she gives you to notify that her husband will be / absence from his house between ten and eleven.
Well, she has received your letter, for which she thanks you a thousand times; and she wants you to know that her husband will be away from his house between ten and eleven.

Ay, forsooth; and then you may come and see the picture, she says, that / you wot of. Master Ford, her husband, will be from home. Alas, the / sweet woman leads an ill life with him. He's a very jealousy man; she / leads a very frampold life with him, good heart.

Yes, truly; and then you can come and see the picture, she says, that you know about. Master Ford, her husband, will be away from home. Alas, the sweet woman has a hard life with him. He's a very jealous man; she has a very troubled life with him, poor heart.
Ten and eleven. Woman, commend me to her; I will not fail her.
Ten and eleven. Woman, give her my regards; I won't let her down.

Why, you say well. But I have another messenger to your worship. / Mistress Page hath her hearty commendations to you too; and let me tell / you in your ear, she's as fartuous a civil modest wife, and one, I tell / you, that will not miss you morning nor evening prayer, as any is in / Windsor, whoe'er be the other; and she bade me tell your worship that / her husband is seldom from home, but she hopes there will come a time. / I never knew a woman so dote upon a man. Surely I think you have / charms, la! Yes, in truth.

Well said. But I have another message for your worship. Mistress Page sends her warm regards to you too; and let me tell you in your ear, she's as virtuous, decent, modest a wife, and one, I tell you, who never misses morning or evening prayer, as any in Windsor, whoever the other may be; and she told me to tell your worship that her husband is seldom away from home, but she hopes a time will come. I never knew a woman so besotted with a man. Surely you must have charms, I'm sure! Yes, truly.
Not I, I assure thee. Setting the attraction of my good parts aside, I / have no other charms.
Not I, I assure you. Apart from the attraction of my good qualities, I have no other charms.
But, I pray thee, tell me this: has Ford's wife and Page's wife / acquainted each other how they love me?
But please tell me this: have Ford's wife and Page's wife told each other that they love me?

That were a jest indeed! They have not so little grace, I hope. That / were a trick indeed! But Mistress Page would desire you to send her / your little page, of all loves. Her husband has a marvellous infection / to the little page; and, truly, Master Page is an honest man. Never a / wife in Windsor leads a better life than she does. Do what she will, / say what she will, take all, pay all, go to bed when she list, rise / when she list, all is as she will, and truly she deserves it, for if / there be a kind woman in Windsor, she is one. You must send her your / page, no remedy.

That would be a joke indeed! I hope they have more sense than that. That would be a fine trick! But Mistress Page begs you, for love's sake, to send her your little page. Her husband has a wonderful affection for the little page; and truly, Master Page is an honest man. No wife in Windsor has a better life than she does. She does what she likes, says what she likes, takes everything, pays for everything, goes to bed when she likes, gets up when she likes; everything is as she wants it, and truly she deserves it, because if there is a kind woman in Windsor, she is one. You must send her your page; there's no way round it.

Nay, but do so then, and, look you, he may come and go between you / both; and in any case have a nay-word, that you may know one another's / mind, and the boy never need to understand anything; for 'tis not good / that children should know any wickedness. Old folks, you know, have / discretion, as they say, and know the world.

Then do so, and, you see, he can go back and forth between you both; and in any case have a password, so you can know each other's minds and the boy never needs to understand anything; because it's not good for children to know about any wickedness. Old people, you know, have discretion, as they say, and know the world.
Fare thee well, commend me to them both. There's my purse; I am yet thy / debtor. Boy, go along with this woman.—This news distracts me.
Goodbye, give them both my regards. Here's my purse; I am still in your debt. Boy, go with this woman. This news drives me wild.
This punk is one of Cupid's carriers; / Clap on more sails, pursue; up with your fights; / Give fire! She is my prize, or ocean whelm them all!
This tart is one of Cupid's cargo ships. Put on more sail, chase her, raise the battle screens, fire! She is my prize, or let the ocean swallow them all!

Sayst thou so, old Jack? Go thy ways, I'll make more of thy old body / than I have done. Will they yet look after thee? Wilt thou, after the / expense of so much money, be now a gainer? Good body, I thank thee. Let / them say 'tis grossly done; so it be fairly done, no matter.

Is that so, old Jack? Go on, I'll make more of your old body than I have done. Will they still pay attention to you? After spending so much money, will you now make a profit? Good body, thank you. Let them say it's done coarsely; as long as it's done well, no matter.
Sir John, there's one Master Brook below would fain speak with you and / be acquainted with you, and hath sent your worship a morning's draught / of sack.
Sir John, there's a Master Brook downstairs who would like to speak with you and get to know you, and he has sent your worship a morning drink of sack.
Such Brooks are welcome to me, that o'erflow such liquor. Ah, ha, / Mistress Ford and Mistress Page, have I encompassed you? Go to, via!
Brooks that overflow with such drink are welcome to me. Aha, Mistress Ford and Mistress Page, have I got you surrounded? Come on, onward!
And you, sir. Would you speak with me?
And you, sir. Do you want to speak with me?
I make bold to press with so little preparation upon you.
I take the liberty of calling on you with so little warning.
You're welcome. What's your will?—Give us leave, drawer.
You're welcome. What do you want? Leave us, waiter.
Sir, I am a gentleman that have spent much. My name is Brook.
Sir, I am a gentleman who has spent a great deal. My name is Brook.
Good Master Brook, I desire more acquaintance of you.
Good Master Brook, I would like to know you better.

Good Sir John, I sue for yours; not to charge you, for I must let you / understand I think myself in better plight for a lender than you are, / the which hath something emboldened me to this unseasoned intrusion; / for they say, if money go before, all ways do lie open.

Good Sir John, I ask the same of you; not to be a burden to you, because I must tell you that I think I'm in a better position to lend than you are, which has made me bold enough for this sudden intrusion. For they say that if money leads the way, all roads lie open.
Money is a good soldier, sir, and will on.
Money is a good soldier, sir, and will push on.
Troth, and I have a bag of money here troubles me. If you will help to / bear it, Sir John, take all, or half, for easing me of the carriage.
Truly, and I have a bag of money here that is bothering me. If you will help me carry it, Sir John, take all of it, or half, to relieve me of the load.
Sir, I know not how I may deserve to be your porter.
Sir, I don't know how I have earned the right to be your porter.
I will tell you, sir, if you will give me the hearing.
I'll tell you, sir, if you'll listen.
Speak, good Master Brook. I shall be glad to be your servant.
Speak, good Master Brook. I'll be glad to serve you.

Sir, I hear you are a scholar—I will be brief with you—and you have / been a man long known to me, though I had never so good means as desire / to make myself acquainted with you. I shall discover a thing to you, / wherein I must very much lay open mine own imperfection. But, good Sir / John, as you have one eye upon my follies, as you hear them unfolded, / turn another into the register of your own, that I may pass with a / reproof the easier, sith you yourself know how easy it is to be such an / offender.

Sir, I hear you are an educated man (I'll be brief with you), and I have known of you for a long time, though I never had the means, only the wish, to get acquainted with you. I am going to reveal something to you in which I must expose my own weakness a great deal. But, good Sir John, while you keep one eye on my follies as you hear them told, turn the other to the record of your own, so that I may get off with a lighter rebuke, since you know yourself how easy it is to commit such an offence.
There is a gentlewoman in this town, her husband's name is Ford.
There is a lady in this town whose husband's name is Ford.

I have long loved her, and, I protest to you, bestowed much on her, / followed her with a doting observance, engrossed opportunities to meet / her, fee'd every slight occasion that could but niggardly give me sight / of her, not only bought many presents to give her, but have given / largely to many to know what she would have given. Briefly, I have / pursued her as love hath pursued me, which hath been on the wing of all / occasions. But whatsoever I have merited, either in my mind or in my / means, meed, I am sure, I have received none, unless experience be a / jewel. That I have purchased at an infinite rate, and that hath taught / me to say this: / Love like a shadow flies when substance love pursues, / Pursuing that that flies, and flying what pursues.

I have loved her for a long time and, I swear to you, spent a great deal on her. I have followed her with devoted attention, seized every chance to meet her, paid for every small occasion that might give me even a stingy glimpse of her, and not only bought her many presents but paid many people generously to find out what she would like to be given. In short, I have chased her as love has chased me, which is on the wings of every opportunity. But whatever I have deserved, in my feelings or my spending, I am sure I have received no reward, unless experience is a jewel. I have bought that at an enormous price, and it has taught me to say this: Love flies like a shadow when real wealth pursues it, chasing what runs away and running from what chases it.
Have you received no promise of satisfaction at her hands?
Have you had no promise of satisfaction from her?
Have you importuned her to such a purpose?
Have you pressed her for it?
Of what quality was your love, then?
What kind of love was yours, then?
Like a fair house built on another man's ground, so that I have lost my / edifice by mistaking the place where I erected it.
Like a fine house built on another man's land, so that I have lost my building by choosing the wrong place to put it up.
To what purpose have you unfolded this to me?
Why have you told me all this?

When I have told you that, I have told you all. Some say that though / she appear honest to me, yet in other places she enlargeth her mirth so / far that there is shrewd construction made of her. Now, Sir John, here / is the heart of my purpose: you are a gentleman of excellent breeding, / admirable discourse, of great admittance, authentic in your place and / person, generally allowed for your many warlike, courtlike, and learned / preparations.

When I've told you that, I've told you everything. Some say that although she seems chaste to me, elsewhere she lets her merriment go so far that people put a bad interpretation on it.
