Now, Sir John, here is the heart of my purpose: you are a gentleman of excellent breeding, wonderful conversation, welcome everywhere, of real standing in rank and person, widely admired for your many military, courtly and learned accomplishments.

Believe it, for you know it. There is money. Spend it, spend it; spend / more; spend all I have; only give me so much of your time in exchange / of it as to lay an amiable siege to the honesty of this Ford's wife. / Use your art of wooing, win her to consent to you. If any man may, you / may as soon as any.

Believe it, because you know it's true. There is money. Spend it, spend it; spend more; spend everything I have; only give me enough of your time in return to lay a loving siege to the virtue of this Ford's wife. Use your skill in wooing and win her consent. If any man can, you can as well as anyone.
Would it apply well to the vehemency of your affection that I should / win what you would enjoy? Methinks you prescribe to yourself very / preposterously.
Would it suit the strength of your passion for me to win what you want to enjoy? It seems to me you are prescribing a very backward treatment for yourself.

O, understand my drift. She dwells so securely on the excellency of her / honour that the folly of my soul dares not present itself; she is too / bright to be looked against. Now, could I come to her with any / detection in my hand, my desires had instance and argument to commend / themselves. I could drive her then from the ward of her purity, her / reputation, her marriage vow, and a thousand other her defences, which / now are too too strongly embattled against me. What say you to't, Sir / John?

Oh, understand my aim. She relies so confidently on her spotless honour that my foolish soul doesn't dare to show itself; she is too bright to look at. But if I could come to her with some proof of guilt in my hand, my desires would have an example and an argument to support them. Then I could drive her out of the fortress of her purity, her reputation, her marriage vows and a thousand other defences of hers, which are now far too strongly ranged against me. What do you say to that, Sir John?
Master Brook, I will first make bold with your money; next, give me / your hand; and last, as I am a gentleman, you shall, if you will, enjoy / Ford's wife.
Master Brook, first I will make free with your money; next, give me your hand; and last, as I am a gentleman, you shall, if you wish, enjoy Ford's wife.
Want no money, Sir John; you shall want none.
Don't go short of money, Sir John; you won't go short.

Want no Mistress Ford, Master Brook; you shall want none. I shall be / with her, I may tell you, by her own appointment; even as you came in / to me, her assistant or go-between parted from me. I say I shall be / with her between ten and eleven, for at that time the jealous rascally / knave her husband will be forth. Come you to me at night. You shall / know how I speed.

Don't go short of Mistress Ford, Master Brook; you won't go short. I'll be with her, I can tell you, at her own invitation; just as you came in to me, her assistant or go-between left me. I tell you I'll be with her between ten and eleven, because at that time her jealous, scoundrelly rogue of a husband will be out. Come to me tonight. You'll hear how I get on.
I am blessed in your acquaintance. Do you know Ford, sir?
I am blessed to know you. Do you know Ford, sir?

Hang him, poor cuckoldly knave! I know him not. Yet I wrong him to call / him poor. They say the jealous wittolly knave hath masses of money, for / the which his wife seems to me well-favoured. I will use her as the key / of the cuckoldly rogue's coffer, and there's my harvest-home.

Hang him, the poor cuckolded rogue! I don't know him. But I wrong him to call him poor. They say the jealous, cuckolded rogue has masses of money, which is why his wife seems pretty to me. I'll use her as the key to the cuckold's money chest, and there's my harvest.
I would you knew Ford, sir, that you might avoid him if you saw him.
I wish you knew Ford, sir, so you could avoid him if you saw him.

Hang him, mechanical salt-butter rogue! I will stare him out of his / wits, I will awe him with my cudgel; it shall hang like a meteor o'er / the cuckold's horns. Master Brook, thou shalt know I will predominate / over the peasant, and thou shalt lie with his wife. Come to me soon at / night. Ford's a knave, and I will aggravate his style. Thou, Master / Brook, shalt know him for knave and cuckold. Come to me soon at night.

Hang him, the vulgar, cheap-butter rogue! I'll stare him out of his wits; I'll scare him with my club; it will hang like a meteor over the cuckold's horns. Master Brook, you'll see I'll get the better of the peasant, and you will sleep with his wife. Come to me tonight. Ford's a knave, and I will add to his titles. You, Master Brook, will know him for knave and cuckold. Come to me tonight.

What a damned epicurean rascal is this! My heart is ready to crack with / impatience. Who says this is improvident jealousy? My wife hath sent to / him, the hour is fixed, the match is made. Would any man have thought / this? See the hell of having a false woman: my bed shall be abused, my / coffers ransacked, my reputation gnawn at; and I shall not only receive / this villanous wrong, but stand under the adoption of abominable terms, / and by him that does me this wrong. Terms, names! Amaimon sounds well; / Lucifer, well; Barbason, well; yet they are devils' additions, the / names of fiends. But cuckold? Wittol? Cuckold? The devil himself hath / not such a name. Page is an ass, a secure ass; he will trust his wife, / he will not be jealous. I will rather trust a Fleming with my butter, / Parson Hugh the Welshman with my cheese, an Irishman with my aqua-vitae / bottle, or a thief to walk my ambling gelding, than my wife with / herself. Then she plots, then she ruminates, then she devises; and what / they think in their hearts they may effect, they will break their / hearts but they will effect. God be praised for my jealousy! Eleven / o'clock the hour. I will prevent this, detect my wife, be revenged on / Falstaff, and laugh at Page. I will about it. Better three hours too / soon than a minute too late. Fie, fie, fie! Cuckold, cuckold, cuckold!

What a damned, pleasure-loving rascal this is! My heart is ready to burst with fury. Who says this is careless jealousy? My wife has sent to him, the hour is fixed, the deal is done. Who would have thought it? See the hell of having an unfaithful wife: my bed will be abused, my money chests ransacked, my reputation gnawed at; and I will not only suffer this vile wrong but be called disgusting names, and by the very man who wrongs me. Names, titles! Amaimon sounds fine; Lucifer, fine; Barbason, fine; yet they are devils' titles, the names of fiends. But cuckold? Willing cuckold? Cuckold? The devil himself has no such name. Page is an ass, an overconfident ass; he will trust his wife, he will not be jealous. I would sooner trust a Dutchman with my butter, Parson Hugh the Welshman with my cheese, an Irishman with my whisky bottle, or a thief to walk my horse, than trust my wife alone with herself. Then she plots, then she broods, then she schemes; and what women think in their hearts they can do, they will break their hearts to do. God be praised for my jealousy! Eleven o'clock is the hour. I will stop this, catch my wife, take revenge on Falstaff and laugh at Page. I'll get to it. Better three hours too early than a minute too late. Shame, shame, shame! Cuckold, cuckold, cuckold!
'Tis past the hour, sir, that Sir Hugh promised to meet.
It's past the time, sir, when Sir Hugh promised to meet you.
By gar, he has save his soul, dat he is no come. He has pray his Pible / well dat he is no come. By gar, Jack Rugby, he is dead already, if he / be come.
By God, he has saved his soul by not coming. He has prayed well from his Bible, since he hasn't come. By God, Jack Rugby, he is a dead man already if he comes.
He is wise, sir; he knew your worship would kill him if he came.
He's wise, sir; he knew your worship would kill him if he came.
By gar, de herring is no dead so as I vill kill him. Take your rapier, / Jack; I vill tell you how I vill kill him.
By God, a herring is not as dead as I will kill him. Take your rapier, Jack; I will show you how I will kill him.
God bless you, my brave doctor!
God save you, Master Doctor Caius!
Vat be all you, one, two, tree, four, come for?
What have you all come for, one, two, three, four of you?

To see thee fight, to see thee foin, to see thee traverse; to see thee / here, to see thee there; to see thee pass thy punto, thy stock, thy / reverse, thy distance, thy montant. Is he dead, my Ethiopian? Is he / dead, my Francisco? Ha, bully? What says my Aesculapius, my Galen, my / heart of elder, ha? Is he dead, bully stale? Is he dead?

To see you fight, to see you thrust, to see you dodge; to see you here, to see you there; to see you make your thrust, your stab, your backhand, your distance, your upward cut. Is he dead, my dark one? Is he dead, my Frenchman? Ha, my lad? What does my god of medicine say, my Galen, my heart of soft wood, ha? Is he dead, my fine piss-pot? Is he dead?
By gar, he is de coward Jack-priest of de vorld. He is not show his / face.
By God, he is the most cowardly rascal of a priest in the world. He hasn't shown his face.
Thou art a Castalion King Urinal Hector of Greece, my boy!
You are a Spanish king of urinals, a Hector of Greece, my boy!
I pray you, bear witness that me have stay six or seven, two, tree / hours for him, and he is no come.
Please bear witness that I have waited six or seven, two, three hours for him, and he hasn't come.
He is the wiser man, Master doctor. He is a curer of souls, and you a / curer of bodies. If you should fight, you go against the hair of your / professions. Is it not true, Master Page?
He's the wiser man, Doctor. He is a healer of souls and you are a healer of bodies. If you fought, you would go against the grain of your professions. Isn't that true, Master Page?
Master Shallow, you have yourself been a great fighter, though now a / man of peace.
Master Shallow, you have been a great fighter yourself, though you're a man of peace now.

Bodykins, Master Page, though I now be old, and of the peace, if I see / a sword out, my finger itches to make one. Though we are justices and / doctors and churchmen, Master Page, we have some salt of our youth in / us. We are the sons of women, Master Page.

By God's body, Master Page, old as I am now, and a Justice of the Peace, if I see a drawn sword my finger itches to join in. Justices, doctors and churchmen as we are, Master Page, we still have some of the salt of our youth in us. We are the sons of women, Master Page.

It will be found so, Master Page.—Master Doctor Caius, I come to fetch / you home. I am sworn of the peace. You have showed yourself a wise / physician, and Sir Hugh hath shown himself a wise and patient / churchman. You must go with me, Master Doctor.

You'll find it so, Master Page. Doctor Caius, I have come to take you home. I am sworn to keep the peace. You have shown yourself a wise physician, and Sir Hugh has shown himself a wise and patient churchman. You must come with me, Doctor.
Pardon, guest justice.—A word, Monsieur Mockwater.
Excuse me, my guest the Justice. A word, Monsieur Mockwater.
Mockwater, in our English tongue, is valour, bully.
Mockwater, in our English tongue, means courage, my lad.
By gar, then I have as much mockvater as de Englishman. Scurvy jack-dog / priest! By gar, me vill cut his ears.
By God, then I have as much mockwater as the Englishman. Lousy cur of a priest! By God, I will cut off his ears.
He will clapper-claw thee tightly, bully.
He will give you a sound thrashing, my lad.
That is, he will make thee amends.
That is, he will apologise to you.
By gar, me do look he shall clapper-de-claw me, for, by gar, me vill / have it.
By God, I expect him to clapper-claw me, because, by God, I will have it.
And I will provoke him to't, or let him wag.
And I will urge him to do it, or let him go hang.
And, moreover, bully—but first, Master guest, and Master Page, and eke / Cavaliero Slender, go you through the town to Frogmore.
And besides, my lad... but first, my guest, and Master Page, and also Sir Slender, go through the town to Frogmore.
[Aside to Host] Sir Hugh is there, is he?
(Aside to Host) Sir Hugh is there, is he?
[Aside to Page] He is there. See what humour he is in; and I will / bring the doctor about by the fields. Will it do well?
(Aside to Page) He's there. See what mood he's in, and I will bring the doctor round by the fields. Will that work?
[Aside to Host] We will do it.
By gar, me vill kill de priest, for he speak for a jackanape to Anne / Page.
By God, I will kill the priest, because he is speaking for a monkey to Anne Page.

Let him die. Sheathe thy impatience; throw cold water on thy choler. Go / about the fields with me through Frogmore. I will bring thee where / Mistress Anne Page is, at a farm-house a-feasting, and thou shalt woo / her. Cried game! Said I well?

Let him die. Put away your impatience; throw cold water on your anger. Come round by the fields with me through Frogmore. I will take you to where Mistress Anne Page is feasting at a farmhouse, and you can woo her. The game is up! Well said?
By gar, me tank you for dat. By gar, I love you; and I shall procure-a / you de good guest: de earl, de knight, de lords, de gentlemen, my / patients.
By God, I thank you for that. By God, I love you; and I will get you good guests: the earl, the knight, the lords, the gentlemen, my patients.
For the which I will be thy adversary toward Anne Page. Said I well?
For which I will be your adversary with Anne Page. Well said?
By God, it is good; well said.
Come at my heels, Jack Rugby.
Follow at my heels, Jack Rugby.
I pray you now, good Master Slender's servingman, and friend Simple by / your name, which way have you looked for Master Caius, that calls / himself doctor of physic?
Please now, good Master Slender's servant, friend Simple by name, which way have you looked for Master Caius, who calls himself a doctor of medicine?
Marry, sir, the Petty-ward, the Park-ward, every way; old Windsor way, / and every way but the town way.
Well, sir, towards the town ward, towards the park, every way; the old Windsor way, and every way except the town way.
I most fehemently desire you, you will also look that way.
I most earnestly ask you to look that way too.

Pless my soul, how full of cholers I am, and trempling of mind! I shall / be glad if he have deceived me. How melancholies I am! I will knog his / urinals about his knave's costard when I have good opportunities for / the 'ork. Pless my soul!

Bless my soul, how full of anger I am, and trembling in my mind! I'll be glad if he has let me down. How melancholy I am! I'll knock his urine flasks about his rascal's head when I have a good chance to do the job. Bless my soul!

To shallow rivers, to whose falls / Melodious birds sings madrigals. / There will we make our peds of roses / And a thousand fragrant posies. / To shallow— / Mercy on me, I have a great dispositions to cry.
To shallow rivers, by whose waterfalls melodious birds sing madrigals. There we will make our beds of roses and a thousand fragrant posies. To shallow... Mercy on me, I have a great urge to cry.
Melodious birds sing madrigals— / Whenas I sat in Pabylon— / And a thousand vagram posies. / To shallow rivers, to whose falls / Melodious birds sing madrigals.
Melodious birds sing madrigals... When I sat in Babylon... And a thousand fragrant posies. To shallow rivers, by whose waterfalls melodious birds sing madrigals.
Yonder he is, coming this way, Sir Hugh.
There he is, coming this way, Sir Hugh.
To shallow rivers, to whose falls—
To shallow rivers, by whose waterfalls...
Heaven prosper the right! What weapons is he?
Heaven favour the right side! What weapons does he have?
No weapons, sir. There comes my master, Master Shallow, and another / gentleman, from Frogmore, over the stile, this way.
No weapons, sir. Here comes my master, Master Shallow, and another gentleman, from Frogmore, over the stile, this way.
Pray you, give me my gown—or else keep it in your arms.
Please give me my gown, or no, keep it in your arms.
How now, Master Parson? Good morrow, good Sir Hugh. Keep a gamester / from the dice, and a good student from his book, and it is wonderful.
Hello, Master Parson! Good morning, good Sir Hugh. Keep a gambler from his dice and a good student from his book, and it's a marvel.
God save you, good Sir Hugh!
God save you, good Sir Hugh!
God pless you from his mercy sake, all of you!
God bless you all, for his mercy's sake!
What, the sword and the word? Do you study them both, Master Parson?
What, the sword and the Bible? Do you study both, Master Parson?
And youthful still—in your doublet and hose, this raw rheumatic day?
And still youthful, in just your jacket and breeches on this raw, damp day?
There is reasons and causes for it.
There are reasons and causes for it.
We are come to you to do a good office, Master Parson.
We have come to you to do a good deed, Master Parson.
Yonder is a most reverend gentleman who, belike having received wrong / by some person, is at most odds with his own gravity and patience that / ever you saw.
Over there is a most respectable gentleman who, apparently having been wronged by someone, is more at odds with his own dignity and patience than you have ever seen.
I have lived fourscore years and upward; I never heard a man of his / place, gravity, and learning, so wide of his own respect.
I have lived eighty years and more, and I never heard of a man of his position, dignity and learning so far from his own self-respect.
I think you know him: Master Doctor Caius, the renowned French / physician.
I think you know him: Doctor Caius, the famous French physician.
Got's will and His passion of my heart! I had as lief you would tell me / of a mess of porridge.
God's will and His passion on my heart! I'd as soon you told me about a bowl of porridge.
He has no more knowledge in Hibbocrates and Galen, and he is a knave / besides, a cowardly knave as you would desires to be acquainted withal.
He knows no more of Hippocrates and Galen than that, and he's a rogue besides, as cowardly a rogue as you could wish to meet.
I warrant you, he's the man should fight with him.
I bet you he's the man who was meant to fight him.
It appears so by his weapons. Keep them asunder. Here comes Doctor / Caius.
It looks like it, from his weapons. Keep them apart. Here comes Doctor Caius.
Nay, good Master Parson, keep in your weapon.
No, good Master Parson, put away your weapon.
So do you, good Master Doctor.
Disarm them, and let them question. Let them keep their limbs whole and / hack our English.
Disarm them and let them argue. Let them keep their limbs in one piece and hack our English instead.
I pray you, let-a me speak a word with your ear. Verefore will you not / meet-a me?
Please, let me have a word in your ear. Why didn't you come to meet me?
[Aside to Caius] Pray you, use your patience. In good time.
(Aside to Caius) Please be patient. All in good time.
By gar, you are de coward, de Jack dog, John ape.
By God, you are a coward, a cur, a monkey.

[Aside to Caius] Pray you, let us not be laughing stocks to other / men's humours. I desire you in friendship, and I will one way or other / make you amends. / [Aloud] By Jeshu, I will knog your urinal about your knave's / cogscomb.

(Aside to Caius) Please, let's not be laughing stocks for other men's amusement. I ask for your friendship, and I will make it up to you one way or another. (Aloud) By Jesus, I'll knock your urine flask about your fool's head.
Diable! Jack Rugby, mine Host de Jarteer, have I not stay for him to / kill him? Have I not, at de place I did appoint?
Devil! Jack Rugby, my landlord of the Garter, haven't I waited for him to kill him? Haven't I, at the place I appointed?
As I am a Christians soul, now look you, this is the place appointed. / I'll be judgment by mine host of the Garter.
As I am a Christian soul, look, this is the place appointed. I'll accept the judgement of my landlord of the Garter.
Peace, I say, Gallia and Gaul, French and Welsh, soul-curer and / body-curer!
Quiet, I say, Gaul and Welshman, French and Welsh, soul-healer and body-healer!
Ay, dat is very good; excellent.
Yes, that is very good; excellent.

Peace, I say! Hear mine host of the Garter. Am I politic? Am I subtle? / Am I a Machiavel? Shall I lose my doctor? No, he gives me the potions / and the motions. Shall I lose my parson, my priest, my Sir Hugh? No, he / gives me the proverbs and the no-verbs. [To Caius] Give me thy hand, / terrestrial; so. [To Evans] Give me thy hand, celestial; so. Boys of / art, I have deceived you both. I have directed you to wrong places. / Your hearts are mighty, your skins are whole, and let burnt sack be the / issue. Come, lay their swords to pawn. Follow me, lads of peace, / follow, follow, follow.

Quiet, I say! Listen to your landlord of the Garter. Am I clever? Am I cunning? Am I a Machiavelli? Shall I lose my doctor? No, he gives me the medicines and the bowel movements. Shall I lose my parson, my priest, my Sir Hugh? No, he gives me the proverbs and the no-verbs. (To Caius) Give me your hand, earthly one; there. (To Evans) Give me your hand, heavenly one; there. Men of learning, I have tricked you both. I sent you to the wrong places. Your hearts are brave, your skins are unbroken, and let hot sack be the outcome. Come, let's pawn their swords. Follow me, lads of peace, follow, follow, follow.
Afore God, a mad host! Follow, gentlemen, follow.
Good God, a mad landlord! Follow, gentlemen, follow.
Ha, do I perceive dat? Have you make-a de sot of us, ha, ha?
Ha, do I see what's going on? Have you made fools of us, ha, ha?

This is well, he has made us his vlouting-stog. I desire you that we / may be friends, and let us knog our prains together to be revenge on / this same scall, scurvy, cogging companion, the host of the Garter.
This is fine: he has made us his laughing stock. I ask that we be friends, and let us put our heads together to get revenge on this scabby, lousy, cheating fellow, the landlord of the Garter.
By gar, with all my heart. He promise to bring me where is Anne Page; / by gar, he deceive me too.
By God, with all my heart. He promised to take me to where Anne Page is; by God, he has tricked me too.
Well, I will smite his noddles. Pray you follow.
Well, I will hit him on the head. Please follow me.
Nay, keep your way, little gallant. You were wont to be a follower, but / now you are a leader. Whether had you rather, lead mine eyes, or eye / your master's heels?
No, go on ahead, little gallant. You used to be a follower, but now you are a leader. Which would you rather do, lead my eyes, or eye your master's heels?
I had rather, forsooth, go before you like a man than follow him like a / dwarf.
Truly, I'd rather walk in front of you like a man than follow him like a dwarf.
O, you are a flattering boy! Now I see you'll be a courtier.
Oh, you're a flattering boy! I can see you'll be a courtier.
Well met, Mistress Page. Whither go you?
Well met, Mistress Page. Where are you going?
Truly, sir, to see your wife. Is she at home?
To see your wife, sir. Is she at home?
Ay, and as idle as she may hang together, for want of company. I think / if your husbands were dead you two would marry.
Yes, and as bored as she can be without falling apart, for lack of company. I think if your husbands were dead, you two would marry each other.
Be sure of that—two other husbands.
You can be sure of that: two other husbands.
Where had you this pretty weathercock?
Where did you get this pretty weathercock?
I cannot tell what the dickens his name is my husband had him of. What / do you call your knight's name, sirrah?
I can't remember what the dickens the name is of the man my husband got him from. What is your knight's name, boy?
He, he; I can never hit on's name. There is such a league between my / good man and he! Is your wife at home indeed?
That's him, that's him; I can never remember his name. There's such a friendship between my husband and him! Is your wife really at home?
By your leave, sir, I am sick till I see her.
Excuse me, sir; I'm sick until I see her.

Has Page any brains? Hath he any eyes? Hath he any thinking? Sure, they / sleep; he hath no use of them. Why, this boy will carry a letter twenty / mile as easy as a cannon will shoot point-blank twelve score. He pieces / out his wife's inclination, he gives her folly motion and advantage. / And now she's going to my wife, and Falstaff's boy with her. A man may / hear this shower sing in the wind. And Falstaff's boy with her! Good / plots they are laid, and our revolted wives share damnation together. / Well, I will take him, then torture my wife, pluck the borrowed veil of / modesty from the so-seeming Mistress Page, divulge Page himself for a / secure and wilful Actaeon, and to these violent proceedings all my / neighbours shall cry aim. [Clock strikes] The clock gives me my cue, / and my assurance bids me search. There I shall find Falstaff. I shall / be rather praised for this than mocked, for it is as positive as the / earth is firm that Falstaff is there. I will go.

Has Page any brains? Has he any eyes? Has he any power of thought? Surely they are asleep; he has no use for them. Why, this boy would carry a letter twenty miles as easily as a cannon shoots point-blank at two hundred and forty yards. He feeds his wife's inclinations; he gives her folly room and opportunity. And now she's going to my wife, with Falstaff's boy. A man can hear this storm coming in the wind. And Falstaff's boy with her! Fine plots they have laid, and our rebellious wives share their damnation together. Well, I will catch him, then torment my wife, pull the borrowed veil of modesty off the so-seemingly virtuous Mistress Page, and expose Page himself as an overconfident and willing cuckold, and all my neighbours will applaud these violent actions. (Clock strikes) The clock gives me my cue, and my certainty tells me to search. I'll find Falstaff there. I'll be praised for this rather than mocked, because it is as certain as the earth is solid that Falstaff is there. I'll go.
Trust me, a good knot. I have good cheer at home, and I pray you all go / with me.
Honestly, a fine group. I have good food at home, and I beg you all to come with me.
I must excuse myself, Master Ford.
I must excuse myself, Master Ford.
And so must I, sir; we have appointed to dine with Mistress Anne, and I / would not break with her for more money than I'll speak of.
And so must I, sir; we have arranged to dine with Mistress Anne, and I wouldn't break my word to her for more money than I'll mention.
We have lingered about a match between Anne Page and my cousin Slender, / and this day we shall have our answer.
We have been slow to settle a match between Anne Page and my cousin Slender, and today we'll get our answer.
I hope I have your good will, father Page.
I hope I have your blessing, father Page.
You have, Master Slender, I stand wholly for you.—But my wife, Master / doctor, is for you altogether.
You do, Master Slender; I'm entirely on your side. But my wife, Doctor, is completely on yours.
Ay, be-gar; and de maid is love-a me! My nursh-a Quickly tell me so / mush.
Yes, by God; and the girl loves me! My nurse Quickly told me so.

What say you to young Master Fenton? He capers, he dances, he has eyes / of youth, he writes verses, he speaks holiday, he smells April and May. / He will carry 't, he will carry 't. 'Tis in his buttons he will carry / 't.

What do you say to young Master Fenton? He capers, he dances, he has young eyes, he writes poems, he talks in holiday style, he smells of April and May. He will win her, he will win her. It is in his nature to win her.

Not by my consent, I promise you. The gentleman is of no having. He / kept company with the wild Prince and Poins. He is of too high a / region, he knows too much. No, he shall not knit a knot in his fortunes / with the finger of my substance. If he take her, let him take her / simply. The wealth I have waits on my consent, and my consent goes not / that way.

Not with my consent, I promise you. The gentleman has no money. He kept company with the wild Prince Hal and Poins. He is of too high a rank, and he knows too much. No, he shall not tie up the loose ends of his fortune with the help of my wealth. If he takes her, let him take her with nothing. My wealth depends on my consent, and my consent doesn't go that way.

I beseech you, heartily, some of you go home with me to dinner. Besides / your cheer, you shall have sport: I will show you a monster. Master / Doctor, you shall go; so shall you, Master Page, and you, Sir Hugh.
I sincerely beg some of you to come home with me to dinner. Besides the food, you'll have some fun: I'll show you a monster. Doctor, you will come; so will you, Master Page, and you, Sir Hugh.
Well, fare you well. We shall have the freer wooing at Master Page's.
Well, goodbye. We'll have freer wooing at Master Page's.
Go home, John Rugby; I come anon.
Go home, John Rugby; I'll come soon.
Farewell, my hearts. I will to my honest knight Falstaff, and drink / canary with him.
Goodbye, my hearties. I'll go to my honest knight Falstaff and drink canary wine with him.
[Aside] I think I shall drink in pipe-wine first with him; I'll make / him dance.—Will you go, gentles?
(Aside) I think I'll make him drink something sharper first; I'll make him dance. Shall we go, gentlemen?
Have with you to see this monster.
We're with you, to see this monster.
Quick, quick! Is the laundry basket—
It's ready, I promise. Robin, come here, I say!
Come on, come on, come on.
Give your men the charge; we must be brief.
Give your men their orders; we must be quick.

Marry, as I told you before, John and Robert, be ready here hard by in / the brew-house; and when I suddenly call you, come forth, and, without / any pause or staggering, take this basket on your shoulders. That done, / trudge with it in all haste, and carry it among the whitsters in / Datchet Mead, and there empty it in the muddy ditch close by the Thames / side.

Well, as I told you before, John and Robert, wait close by here in the brew-house; and when I suddenly call you, come out and, without stopping or stumbling, lift this basket onto your shoulders. Then hurry off with it as fast as you can, carry it to the women bleaching linen in Datchet Meadow, and empty it into the muddy ditch beside the Thames.
I ha' told them over and over, they lack no direction.—Be gone, and / come when you are called.
I've told them over and over; they don't need any more instructions. Go, and come when you're called.
How now, my eyas-musket, what news with you?
Well, my little sparrowhawk, what news do you have?
My Master, Sir John, is come in at your back door, Mistress Ford, and / requests your company.
My master, Sir John, has come in at your back door, Mistress Ford, and asks for your company.
You little Jack-a-Lent, have you been true to us?
You little puppet, have you been loyal to us?
Ay, I'll be sworn. My master knows not of your being here, and hath / threatened to put me into everlasting liberty if I tell you of it; for / he swears he'll turn me away.
Yes, I swear it. My master doesn't know you're here, and he has threatened to give me everlasting freedom if I tell you about it, because he swears he'll sack me.
Thou'rt a good boy, this secrecy of thine shall be a tailor to thee, / and shall make thee a new doublet and hose. I'll go hide me.
You're a good boy. This secret of yours will be your tailor and make you a new jacket and breeches. I'll go and hide.
Do so.—Go tell thy master I am alone.
Do. Go and tell your master I'm alone.
Mistress Page, remember you your cue.
I warrant thee. If I do not act it, hiss me.
I promise you. If I don't play my part, hiss me off.
Go to, then. We'll use this unwholesome humidity, this gross watery / pumpion; we'll teach him to know turtles from jays.
Go on, then. We'll deal with this unhealthy bag of moisture, this great watery pumpkin; we'll teach him to tell faithful turtledoves from chattering jays.
"Have I caught thee, my heavenly jewel?" Why, now let me die, for I / have lived long enough. This is the period of my ambition. O this / blessed hour!
"Have I caught you, my heavenly jewel?" Why, now let me die, for I have lived long enough. This is the summit of my ambition. Oh, this blessed hour!
Mistress Ford, I cannot cog, I cannot prate, Mistress Ford. Now shall I / sin in my wish: I would thy husband were dead. I'll speak it before the / best lord: I would make thee my lady.
Mistress Ford, I can't flatter, I can't chatter, Mistress Ford. Now I'll sin in my wish: I wish your husband were dead. I'd say it in front of the greatest lord: I would make you my lady.
I your lady, Sir John? Alas, I should be a pitiful lady.
Me, your lady, Sir John? Oh dear, I'd be a pitiful lady.

Let the court of France show me such another. I see how thine eye would / emulate the diamond. Thou hast the right arched beauty of the brow that / becomes the ship-tire, the tire-valiant, or any tire of Venetian / admittance.

Let the French court show me another like you. I can see how your eyes would rival a diamond. You have just the right arched beauty of the forehead to suit a ship-shaped headdress, a fancy headdress, or any headdress in the Venetian fashion.
A plain kerchief, Sir John. My brows become nothing else, nor that well / neither.
A plain headscarf, Sir John. Nothing else suits my forehead, and that doesn't suit it very well either.

By the Lord, thou art a traitor to say so. Thou wouldst make an / absolute courtier, and the firm fixture of thy foot would give an / excellent motion to thy gait in a semi-circled farthingale. I see what / thou wert, if Fortune thy foe were not, Nature thy friend. Come, thou / canst not hide it.

By the Lord, you are a traitor to say so. You'd make a perfect lady of the court, and the firm way you set your foot would give your walk an excellent motion in a hooped skirt. I can see what you would be, if Fortune were not your enemy when Nature is your friend. Come, you can't hide it.
Believe me, there's no such thing in me.
Believe me, there's nothing like that in me.

What made me love thee? Let that persuade thee there's something / extraordinary in thee. Come, I cannot cog and say thou art this and / that, like a many of these lisping hawthorn buds that come like women / in men's apparel, and smell like Bucklersbury in simple-time. I cannot. / But I love thee, none but thee; and thou deservest it.

What made me love you? Let that convince you there's something extraordinary in you. Come, I can't flatter and say you are this and that, like so many of these lisping young dandies who come dressed up like women in men's clothes and smell like a herb shop in summer. I can't. But I love you, no one but you, and you deserve it.
Do not betray me, sir; I fear you love Mistress Page.
Don't deceive me, sir; I'm afraid you love Mistress Page.
Thou mightst as well say I love to walk by the Counter gate, which is / as hateful to me as the reek of a lime-kiln.
You might as well say I love walking past the debtors' prison gate, which I hate as much as the stink of a lime-kiln.
Well, heaven knows how I love you, and you shall one day find it.
Well, heaven knows how I love you, and one day you will find out.
Keep in that mind, I'll deserve it.
Keep thinking that way; I'll deserve it.
Nay, I must tell you, so you do; or else I could not be in that mind.
Well, I must tell you, you do deserve it, or I couldn't think that way.
Mistress Ford, Mistress Ford, here's Mistress Page at the door, / sweating and blowing and looking wildly, and would needs speak with you / presently.
Mistress Ford, Mistress Ford, Mistress Page is at the door, sweating and panting and looking wild, and she must speak to you at once.
She shall not see me; I will ensconce me behind the arras.
She mustn't see me; I'll hide behind the tapestry.
Pray you, do so; she's a very tattling woman.
Please do; she's a terrible gossip.
What's the matter? What is it?
O Mistress Ford, what have you done? You're shamed, you're overthrown, / you're undone for ever!
Oh, Mistress Ford, what have you done? You're disgraced, you're ruined, you're finished for ever!
What's the matter, good Mistress Page?
What's the matter, good Mistress Page?
O well-a-day, Mistress Ford, having an honest man to your husband, to / give him such cause of suspicion!
Oh, alas, Mistress Ford, when you have an honest man for a husband, to give him such cause for suspicion!
What cause of suspicion? Out upon you! How am I mistook in you!
What cause for suspicion? Shame on you! How wrong I was about you!
Why, oh dear, what's the matter?

Your husband's coming hither, woman, with all the officers in Windsor, / to search for a gentleman that he says is here now in the house, by / your consent, to take an ill advantage of his absence. You are undone.

Your husband is coming here, woman, with all the officers in Windsor, to search for a gentleman who he says is in the house right now with your consent, to take wicked advantage of his absence. You're ruined.

Pray heaven it be not so, that you have such a man here! But 'tis most / certain your husband's coming, with half Windsor at his heels, to / search for such a one. I come before to tell you. If you know yourself / clear, why, I am glad of it; but if you have a friend here, convey, / convey him out. Be not amazed, call all your senses to you; defend your / reputation, or bid farewell to your good life for ever.

Pray heaven it isn't true that you have such a man here! But it's absolutely certain your husband is coming, with half of Windsor at his heels, to search for such a man. I came ahead to tell you. If you know you're innocent, why, I'm glad; but if you have a friend here, get him out, get him out. Don't panic; gather your wits; defend your reputation, or say goodbye to your good life for ever.
What shall I do? There is a gentleman, my dear friend; and I fear not / mine own shame as much as his peril. I had rather than a thousand pound / he were out of the house.
What shall I do? There is a gentleman here, my dear friend; and I'm not as afraid of my own shame as of his danger. I'd give a thousand pounds to have him out of the house.

For shame! Never stand "you had rather" and "you had rather". Your / husband's here at hand. Bethink you of some conveyance. In the house / you cannot hide him. O, how have you deceived me! Look, here is a / basket. If he be of any reasonable stature, he may creep in here; and / throw foul linen upon him, as if it were going to bucking. Or—it is / whiting-time—send him by your two men to Datchet Mead.

For shame! Don't stand there saying "I'd give" and "I'd give". Your husband is close by. Think of some way to get him out. You can't hide him in the house. Oh, how you have deceived me! Look, here is a basket. If he's of any reasonable size, he can creep in here; then throw dirty linen over him, as if it were going to the wash. Or, since it's bleaching time, send him with your two men to Datchet Meadow.
He's too big to go in there. What shall I do?
He's too big to get in there. What shall I do?
[Comes out of hiding] Let me see 't, let me see 't! O, let me see / 't! I'll in, I'll in. Follow your friend's counsel. I'll in.
(Coming out of hiding) Let me see it, let me see it! Oh, let me see it! I'll get in, I'll get in. Take your friend's advice. I'll get in.
What, Sir John Falstaff? Are these your letters, knight?
What, Sir John Falstaff? Are these your letters, knight?
I love thee, and none but thee. Help me away. Let me creep in here. / I'll never—
I love you, and no one but you. Help me get away. Let me creep in here. I'll never—
Help to cover your master, boy.—Call your men, Mistress Ford.—You / dissembling knight!
Help cover your master, boy. Call your men, Mistress Ford. You lying knight!
Go, take up these clothes here, quickly. Where's the cowl-staff? Look / how you drumble! Carry them to the laundress in Datchet Mead; quickly, / come.
Go on, pick up these clothes here, quickly. Where's the carrying pole? Look how you dawdle! Take them to the laundress in Datchet Meadow; quickly, come on.
Pray you come near. If I suspect without cause, why then make sport at / me, then let me be your jest; I deserve it.—How now? Whither bear you / this?
Please come in. If I suspect without cause, then laugh at me, make me your joke; I'll deserve it. What's this? Where are you taking this?
Why, what have you to do whither they bear it? You were best meddle / with buck-washing!
Why, what business is it of yours where they take it? You'd better leave the washing to us!
Buck? I would I could wash myself of the buck! Buck, buck, buck! Ay, / buck! I warrant you, buck, and of the season too, it shall appear.
Buck-washing? I wish I could wash myself clean of the buck! Buck, buck, buck! Yes, buck! I promise you, a horned buck, and in the rutting season too, as you'll see.

Gentlemen, I have dreamed tonight; I'll tell you my dream. Here, here, / here be my keys. Ascend my chambers, search, seek, find out. I'll / warrant we'll unkennel the fox. Let me stop this way first. [Locks the / door.] So, now uncape.

Gentlemen, I had a dream last night; I'll tell you my dream. Here, here, here are my keys. Go up to my rooms, search, look, find him. I bet we'll drive the fox out of his hole. Let me block this way first. (Locks the door) There, now start the hunt.
Good Master Ford, be contented: you wrong yourself too much.
Good Master Ford, calm down; you do yourself too much wrong.
True, Master Page.—Up, gentlemen, you shall see sport anon. Follow me, / gentlemen.
True, Master Page. Upstairs, gentlemen; you'll see some sport soon. Follow me, gentlemen.
This is fery fantastical humours and jealousies.
These are very fantastic moods and jealousies.
By gar, 'tis no the fashion of France; it is not jealous in France.
By God, it is not the fashion in France; nobody is jealous in France.
Nay, follow him, gentlemen; see the issue of his search.
Well, follow him, gentlemen; let's see how his search turns out.
Is there not a double excellency in this?
I know not which pleases me better, that my husband is deceived, or Sir / John.
I don't know which pleases me more, that my husband is fooled, or Sir John.
What a taking was he in when your husband asked who was in the basket!
What a state he was in when your husband asked what was in the basket!
I am half afraid he will have need of washing, so throwing him into the / water will do him a benefit.
I'm half afraid he'll need a wash, so throwing him in the water will do him good.
Hang him, dishonest rascal! I would all of the same strain were in the / same distress.
Hang him, the lecherous rascal! I wish everyone of his kind were in the same trouble.
I think my husband hath some special suspicion of Falstaff's being / here, for I never saw him so gross in his jealousy till now.
I think my husband has some particular suspicion that Falstaff is here, because I've never seen him so wildly jealous until now.
I will lay a plot to try that, and we will yet have more tricks with / Falstaff. His dissolute disease will scarce obey this medicine.
I'll lay a plan to test that, and we'll play more tricks on Falstaff yet. His lustful disease will hardly be cured by this one dose.
Shall we send that foolish carrion Mistress Quickly to him, and excuse / his throwing into the water, and give him another hope, to betray him / to another punishment?
Shall we send that foolish old bag Mistress Quickly to him, to apologise for his being thrown into the water and give him new hope, so we can lure him into another punishment?
We will do it. Let him be sent for tomorrow eight o'clock to have / amends.
We'll do it. Let him be invited tomorrow at eight o'clock, to make up for it.
I cannot find him. Maybe the knave bragged of that he could not / compass.
I can't find him. Perhaps the rogue boasted of something he couldn't manage.
[Aside to Mistress Ford] Heard you that?
(Aside to Mistress Ford) Did you hear that?
You use me well, Master Ford, do you?
You treat me well, Master Ford, don't you?
Heaven make you better than your thoughts!
Heaven make you better than your thoughts!
You do yourself mighty wrong, Master Ford.
You do yourself great wrong, Master Ford.
Ay, ay; I must bear it.
Yes, yes; I must put up with it.
If there be anypody in the house, and in the chambers, and in the / coffers, and in the presses, heaven forgive my sins at the day of / judgment!
If there's anybody in the house, in the bedrooms, in the chests or in the cupboards, may heaven forgive my sins on Judgement Day!
Be gar, nor I too; there is nobodies.
By God, nor me either; there is nobody.
Fie, fie, Master Ford, are you not ashamed? What spirit, what devil / suggests this imagination? I would not ha' your distemper in this kind / for the wealth of Windsor Castle.
Shame, shame, Master Ford, aren't you ashamed? What spirit, what devil puts this idea in your head? I wouldn't have your sickness of this kind for all the wealth of Windsor Castle.
'Tis my fault, Master Page. I suffer for it.
It's my fault, Master Page. I suffer for it.
You suffer for a pad conscience. Your wife is as honest a 'omans as I / will desires among five thousand, and five hundred too.
You suffer for a bad conscience. Your wife is as faithful a woman as I could wish for among five thousand, and five hundred more.
By gar, I see 'tis an honest woman.
By God, I see she is an honest woman.

Well, I promised you a dinner. Come, come, walk in the park. I pray you / pardon me; I will hereafter make known to you why I have done this. / Come, wife, come, Mistress Page, I pray you pardon me. Pray heartily, / pardon me.

Well, I promised you a dinner. Come, come, let's walk in the park. Please forgive me; later I'll tell you why I have done this. Come, wife; come, Mistress Page; please forgive me. Please, with all my heart, forgive me.
Let's go in, gentlemen; but, trust me, we'll mock him. I do invite you / tomorrow morning to my house to breakfast; after, we'll a-birding / together; I have a fine hawk for the bush. Shall it be so?

Let's go in, gentlemen; but, believe me, we'll make fun of him. I invite you to my house for breakfast tomorrow morning; afterwards we'll go bird hunting together; I have a fine hawk for hunting in the bushes. Shall we?
If there is one, I shall make two in the company.
If there is one, I will make two in the party.
If there be one or two, I shall make-a the turd.
If there are one or two, I will make the third.
I pray you now, remembrance tomorrow on the lousy knave, mine host.
Please, now, remember tomorrow about that lousy rogue, our landlord.
Dat is good, by gar, with all my heart.
That is good, by God, with all my heart.
A lousy knave, to have his gibes and his mockeries!
A lousy rogue, with his jokes and his mockery!
I see I cannot get thy father's love; / Therefore no more turn me to him, sweet Nan.
I see I can't win your father's love, so don't send me to him any more, sweet Nan.

Why, thou must be thyself. / He doth object I am too great of birth, / And that my state being galled with my expense, / I seek to heal it only by his wealth. / Besides these, other bars he lays before me: / My riots past, my wild societies— / And tells me 'tis a thing impossible / I should love thee but as a property.

Why, you must be yourself and choose. He objects that I am of too high a birth, and that with my estate damaged by my spending, I am only trying to mend it with his money. Besides these, he puts other obstacles in my way: my wild past, my rowdy companions; and he tells me it is impossible that I could love you except as property.
Perhaps he's telling you the truth.

No, heaven so speed me in my time to come! / Albeit I will confess thy father's wealth / Was the first motive that I wooed thee, Anne, / Yet, wooing thee, I found thee of more value / Than stamps in gold or sums in sealed bags. / And 'tis the very riches of thyself / That now I aim at.

No, so help me heaven in the time to come! Though I admit your father's wealth was the first reason I wooed you, Anne, yet as I wooed you I found you worth more than stamped gold or sums in sealed bags. And it is the true riches of yourself that I am after now.
Gentle Master Fenton, / Yet seek my father's love, still seek it, sir. / If opportunity and humblest suit / Cannot attain it, why then—hark you hither.
Gentle Master Fenton, still try to win my father's love; keep trying, sir. If opportunity and the humblest pleading can't win it, why then... listen here.
Break their talk, Mistress Quickly. My kinsman shall speak for himself.
Break up their talk, Mistress Quickly. My kinsman will speak for himself.
I'll make a shaft or a bolt on 't. 'Slid, 'tis but venturing.
I'll have a try one way or another. By God's eyelid, it's only a risk.
No, she shall not dismay me. I care not for that, but that I am afeard.
No, she won't make me lose heart. I don't care about that, except that I'm scared.
Hark ye, Master Slender would speak a word with you.
Listen, Master Slender would like a word with you.
I come to him. / [Aside] This is my father's choice. / O, what a world of vile ill-favoured faults / Looks handsome in three hundred pounds a year!
I'm coming to him. (Aside) This is my father's choice. Oh, what a world of vile, ugly faults looks handsome with three hundred pounds a year!
And how does good Master Fenton? Pray you, a word with you.
And how is good Master Fenton? Please, a word with you.
[To Slender] She's coming; to her, coz. O boy, thou hadst a father!
(To Slender) She's coming; go to her, cousin. Oh boy, remember you had a father!
I had a father, Mistress Anne; my uncle can tell you good jests of / him.—Pray you, uncle, tell Mistress Anne the jest how my father stole / two geese out of a pen, good uncle.
I had a father, Mistress Anne; my uncle can tell you good jokes about him. Please, uncle, tell Mistress Anne the joke about how my father stole two geese out of a pen, good uncle.
Mistress Anne, my cousin loves you.
Mistress Anne, my cousin loves you.
Ay, that I do, as well as I love any woman in Gloucestershire.
Yes, I do, as much as I love any woman in Gloucestershire.
He will maintain you like a gentlewoman.
He will keep you like a gentlewoman.
Ay, that I will, come cut and long-tail, under the degree of a squire.
Yes, I will, come what may, as well as anyone below the rank of squire.
He will make you a hundred and fifty pounds jointure.
He will settle a hundred and fifty pounds on you as your widow's share.
Good Master Shallow, let him woo for himself.
Good Master Shallow, let him woo for himself.
Marry, I thank you for it, I thank you for that good comfort.—She calls / you, coz; I'll leave you.
Well, thank you for that, thank you for that encouragement. She's calling you, cousin; I'll leave you.
My will? 'Od's heartlings, that's a pretty jest indeed! I ne'er made my / will yet, I thank heaven. I am not such a sickly creature, I give / heaven praise.
My will? By God's little heart, that's a good joke indeed! I haven't made my will yet, thank heaven. I'm not such a sickly creature, heaven be praised.
I mean, Master Slender, what would you with me?
I mean, Master Slender, what do you want with me?

Truly, for mine own part I would little or nothing with you. Your / father and my uncle hath made motions. If it be my luck, so; if not, / happy man be his dole. They can tell you how things go better than I / can. You may ask your father. Here he comes.

Honestly, for my own part I want little or nothing with you. Your father and my uncle have made proposals. If I'm lucky, fine; if not, good luck to the winner. They can tell you how things stand better than I can. You can ask your father. Here he comes.
Now, Master Slender.—Love him, daughter Anne.— / Why, how now? What does Master Fenton here? / You wrong me, sir, thus still to haunt my house. / I told you, sir, my daughter is disposed of.
Now then, Master Slender. Love him, daughter Anne. Why, what's this? What is Master Fenton doing here? You wrong me, sir, by haunting my house like this. I told you, sir, my daughter is spoken for.
Nay, Master Page, be not impatient.
Now, Master Page, don't be impatient.
Good Master Fenton, come not to my child.
Good Master Fenton, don't come after my child.
She is no match for you.
She's not a match for you.
No, good Master Fenton.— / Come, Master Shallow; come, son Slender, in.— / Knowing my mind, you wrong me, Master Fenton.
No, good Master Fenton. Come, Master Shallow; come in, son Slender. You know my mind, so you wrong me, Master Fenton.

Good Mistress Page, for that I love your daughter / In such a righteous fashion as I do, / Perforce, against all checks, rebukes, and manners, / I must advance the colours of my love / And not retire. Let me have your good will.

Good Mistress Page, because I love your daughter as honourably as I do, I am forced, in spite of all setbacks, rebukes and good manners, to march forward under the flag of my love and not retreat. Let me have your goodwill.
Good mother, do not marry me to yond fool.
Good mother, don't marry me to that fool.
I mean it not; I seek you a better husband.
I don't mean to; I'm looking for a better husband for you.
Alas, I had rather be set quick i' th' earth, / And bowled to death with turnips.
Oh no, I'd rather be buried alive and pelted to death with turnips.

Come, trouble not yourself, good Master Fenton, / I will not be your friend, nor enemy. / My daughter will I question how she loves you, / And as I find her, so am I affected. / Till then, farewell, sir. She must needs go in; / Her father will be angry.

Come, don't trouble yourself, good Master Fenton. I will be neither your friend nor your enemy. I'll ask my daughter how much she loves you, and my feelings will follow what I find. Until then, goodbye, sir. She must go in; her father will be angry.
This is my doing now. "Nay," said I, "will you cast away your child on / a fool, and a physician? Look on Master Fenton." This is my doing.
This is my doing now. "No," I said, "will you throw your child away on a fool, or a physician? Look at Master Fenton." This is my doing.
I thank thee; and I pray thee, once tonight / Give my sweet Nan this ring. There's for thy pains.
Thank you; and please, some time tonight, give my sweet Nan this ring. That's for your trouble.
Now Heaven send thee good fortune!
Now heaven send you good luck!

A kind heart he hath. A woman would run through fire and water for such / a kind heart. But yet I would my master had Mistress Anne, or I would / Master Slender had her; or, in sooth, I would Master Fenton had her. I / will do what I can for them all three, for so I have promised and I'll / be as good as my word—but speciously for Master Fenton. Well, I must of / another errand to Sir John Falstaff from my two mistresses. What a / beast am I to slack it!

He has a kind heart. A woman would go through fire and water for such a kind heart. But still, I wish my master had Mistress Anne; or I wish Master Slender had her; or, honestly, I wish Master Fenton had her. I'll do what I can for all three of them, because that's what I promised, and I'll be as good as my word, but especially for Master Fenton. Well, I must go on another errand to Sir John Falstaff from my two ladies. What a beast I am to be so slow about it!
Go fetch me a quart of sack; put a toast in 't.
Go and get me a quart of sack; put some toast in it.

Have I lived to be carried in a basket like a barrow of butcher's / offal, and to be thrown in the Thames? Well, if I be served such / another trick, I'll have my brains ta'en out and buttered, and give / them to a dog for a New Year's gift. 'Sblood, the rogues slighted me / into the river with as little remorse as they would have drowned a / blind bitch's puppies, fifteen i' the litter; and you may know by my / size that I have a kind of alacrity in sinking; if the bottom were as / deep as hell, I should down. I had been drowned, but that the shore was / shelvy and shallow—a death that I abhor, for the water swells a man, / and what a thing should I have been when I had been swelled! I should / have been a mountain of mummy.

Have I lived to be carried in a basket like a barrowful of butcher's scraps and thrown in the Thames? Well, if I'm served another trick like that, I'll have my brains taken out and buttered and give them to a dog as a New Year's present. By God's blood, the rogues tipped me into the river with as little pity as if they were drowning a blind bitch's puppies, fifteen in the litter; and you can tell by my size that I have a sort of talent for sinking. If the bottom were as deep as hell, I'd go down. I would have drowned if the shore hadn't been sloping and shallow, a death I loathe, because water makes a man swell, and what a sight I would have been swollen! I'd have been a mountain of mummified flesh.
Here's Mistress Quickly, sir, to speak with you.
Mistress Quickly is here, sir, to speak with you.
Come, let me pour in some sack to the Thames water, for my belly's as / cold as if I had swallowed snowballs for pills to cool the reins. Call / her in.
Come, let me pour some sack in on top of the Thames water, because my belly is as cold as if I'd swallowed snowballs as pills to cool my lust. Send her in.
By your leave, I cry you mercy. Give your worship good morrow.
Excuse me, I beg your pardon. Good morning to your worship.
Take away these chalices. Go, brew me a pottle of sack finely.
Take away these cups. Go and make me a half-gallon of hot sack, nicely.
Simple of itself. I'll no pullet sperm in my brewage.
Plain, on its own. I'll have no chicken sperm in my drink.
Marry, sir, I come to your worship from Mistress Ford.
Well, sir, I come to your worship from Mistress Ford.
Mistress Ford? I have had ford enough. I was thrown into the ford, I / have my belly full of ford.
Mistress Ford? I've had enough of fords. I was thrown into the ford; I have a bellyful of ford.
Alas the day, good heart, that was not her fault. She does so take on / with her men; they mistook their erection.
Oh dear, good heart, that wasn't her fault. She is so angry with her men; they misunderstood their erection, I mean direction.
So did I mine, to build upon a foolish woman's promise.
So did I mine, building on a foolish woman's promise.

Well, she laments, sir, for it, that it would yearn your heart to see / it. Her husband goes this morning a-birding; she desires you once more / to come to her, between eight and nine. I must carry her word quickly. / She'll make you amends, I warrant you.

Well, she's so sorry for it, sir, it would melt your heart to see it. Her husband goes bird hunting this morning; she begs you to come to her once more, between eight and nine. I must take her your answer quickly. She'll make it up to you, I promise.
Well, I will visit her. Tell her so, and bid her think what a man is. / Let her consider his frailty, and then judge of my merit.
Well, I'll visit her. Tell her so, and tell her to think what a man is. Let her consider his weakness, and then judge how much I deserve.
Do so. Between nine and ten, sayst thou?
Do. Between nine and ten, you say?
Well, be gone. I will not miss her.
Well, go. I won't miss her.
I marvel I hear not of Master Brook; he sent me word to stay within. I / like his money well. O, here he comes.
I'm surprised I haven't heard from Master Brook; he sent word that I should stay in. I like his money a lot. Oh, here he comes.
Now, Master Brook, you come to know what hath passed between me and / Ford's wife?
Well, Master Brook, you've come to find out what has happened between me and Ford's wife?
That indeed, Sir John, is my business.
That is indeed my business, Sir John.
Master Brook, I will not lie to you. I was at her house the hour she / appointed me.
Master Brook, I won't lie to you. I was at her house at the hour she gave me.
And how did you get on, sir?
How so, sir? Did she change her determination?
How was that, sir? Did she change her mind?

No. Master Brook, but the peaking cornuto her husband, Master Brook, / dwelling in a continual 'larum of jealousy, comes me in the instant of / our encounter, after we had embraced, kissed, protested, and, as it / were, spoke the prologue of our comedy; and at his heels a rabble of / his companions, thither provoked and instigated by his distemper, and, / forsooth, to search his house for his wife's love.

No, Master Brook; but her sneaking cuckold of a husband, Master Brook, who lives in a constant alarm of jealousy, came in at the very moment of our meeting, after we had embraced, kissed, made our vows and, so to speak, spoken the prologue of our comedy; and at his heels came a rabble of his friends, stirred up and brought there by his madness, to search his house, if you please, for his wife's lover.
And did he search for you, and could not find you?
And he searched for you and couldn't find you?

You shall hear. As good luck would have it, comes in one Mistress Page, / gives intelligence of Ford's approach; and, in her invention and Ford's / wife's distraction, they conveyed me into a buck-basket.
You'll hear. As luck would have it, in comes a Mistress Page, who brings news that Ford is coming; and through her quick thinking and Ford's wife's panic, they smuggled me into a laundry basket.

By the Lord, a buck-basket! Rammed me in with foul shirts and smocks, / socks, foul stockings, greasy napkins, that, Master Brook, there was / the rankest compound of villainous smell that ever offended nostril.

By the Lord, a laundry basket! They rammed me in with dirty shirts and petticoats, socks, dirty stockings and greasy napkins, so that, Master Brook, there was the foulest mixture of vile smells that ever offended a nostril.
And how long lay you there?
And how long did you lie there?

Nay, you shall hear, Master Brook, what I have suffered to bring this / woman to evil for your good. Being thus crammed in the basket, a couple / of Ford's knaves, his hinds, were called forth by their mistress to / carry me in the name of foul clothes to Datchet Lane. They took me on / their shoulders, met the jealous knave their master in the door, who / asked them once or twice what they had in their basket. I quaked for / fear lest the lunatic knave would have searched it; but Fate, ordaining / he should be a cuckold, held his hand. Well, on went he for a search, / and away went I for foul clothes. But mark the sequel, Master Brook. I / suffered the pangs of three several deaths: first, an intolerable / fright to be detected with a jealous rotten bell-wether; next, to be / compassed like a good bilbo in the circumference of a peck, hilt to / point, heel to head; and then, to be stopped in, like a strong / distillation, with stinking clothes that fretted in their own grease. / Think of that, a man of my kidney, think of that—that am as subject to / heat as butter; a man of continual dissolution and thaw. It was a / miracle to 'scape suffocation. And in the height of this bath, when I / was more than half stewed in grease, like a Dutch dish, to be thrown / into the Thames and cooled, glowing hot, in that surge, like a / horseshoe! Think of that—hissing hot—think of that, Master Brook.

Now, you'll hear, Master Brook, what I have suffered trying to lead this woman astray for your benefit. Crammed into the basket like that, I was carried by a couple of Ford's servants, his farmhands, whom their mistress called to take me as dirty clothes to Datchet Lane. They lifted me onto their shoulders and met their jealous rogue of a master at the door, who asked them once or twice what they had in their basket. I shook with fear that the lunatic would search it; but Fate, having decided he would be a cuckold, held back his hand. Well, off he went to search, and off I went as dirty clothes. But listen to what followed, Master Brook. I suffered the agonies of three separate deaths: first, the unbearable fright of being caught by a jealous, rotten old ram; next, being bent like a good sword into the round of a bucket, hilt to point, heel to head; and then being sealed in, like a strong brew in a still, with stinking clothes fermenting in their own grease. Think of that, a man of my build, think of that, who melts in the heat like butter, a man always dissolving and thawing. It was a miracle I didn't suffocate. And at the height of this bath, when I was more than half stewed in grease like a Dutch dish, to be thrown into the Thames and cooled, glowing hot, in the waves, like a horseshoe! Think of that, hissing hot; think of that, Master Brook.
In good sadness, sir, I am sorry that for my sake you have suffered all / this. My suit, then, is desperate. You'll undertake her no more?
In all seriousness, sir, I'm sorry you've suffered all this for my sake. My suit is hopeless, then. You won't try her any more?

Master Brook, I will be thrown into Etna, as I have been into Thames, / ere I will leave her thus. Her husband is this morning gone a-birding; / I have received from her another embassy of meeting. 'Twixt eight and / nine is the hour, Master Brook.

Master Brook, I'll let myself be thrown into Mount Etna, as I was into the Thames, before I give her up like this. Her husband has gone bird hunting this morning; I have had another message from her arranging a meeting. Between eight and nine is the time, Master Brook.

Is it? I will then address me to my appointment. Come to me at your / convenient leisure, and you shall know how I speed; and the conclusion / shall be crowned with your enjoying her. Adieu. You shall have her, / Master Brook. Master Brook, you shall cuckold Ford.

Is it? Then I'll be off to my appointment. Come to me when it suits you, and you'll hear how I get on; and the end of it will be crowned by your enjoying her. Goodbye. You'll have her, Master Brook. Master Brook, you'll make a cuckold of Ford.

Hum! Ha! Is this a vision? Is this a dream? Do I sleep? Master Ford, / awake; awake, Master Ford! There's a hole made in your best coat, / Master Ford. This 'tis to be married; this 'tis to have linen and / buck-baskets! Well, I will proclaim myself what I am. I will now take / the lecher. He is at my house. He cannot scape me. 'Tis impossible he / should. He cannot creep into a half-penny purse, nor into a pepperbox. / But, lest the devil that guides him should aid him, I will search / impossible places. Though what I am I cannot avoid, yet to be what I / would not shall not make me tame. If I have horns to make one mad, let / the proverb go with me: I'll be horn-mad.

Hmm! Ha! Is this a vision? Is this a dream? Am I asleep? Master Ford, wake up; wake up, Master Ford! There's a hole in your best coat, Master Ford. This is what it is to be married; this is what it is to have linen and laundry baskets! Well, I'll announce myself for what I am. Now I'll catch the lecher. He's at my house. He can't escape me. It's impossible. He can't creep into a halfpenny purse, or into a pepper pot. But in case the devil who guides him helps him, I'll search impossible places. Though I can't avoid being what I am, being what I don't want to be won't make me meek. If I have horns to drive a man mad, let the proverb fit me: I'll be horn-mad.
Is he at Master Ford's already, think'st thou?
Do you think he's at Master Ford's already?
Sure he is by this; or will be presently. But truly he is very / courageous mad about his throwing into the water. Mistress Ford desires / you to come suddenly.
He's sure to be by now, or will be soon. But honestly, he's furious about being thrown into the water. Mistress Ford wants you to come at once.
I'll be with her by and by. I'll but bring my young man here to school. / Look where his master comes; 'tis a playing day, I see.
I'll be with her soon. I'm just taking my young man here to school. Look, here comes his teacher; it's a holiday, I see.
How now, Sir Hugh, no school today?
Hello, Sir Hugh, no school today?
No, Master Slender is let the boys leave to play.
No, Master Slender has got the boys a holiday to play.
Sir Hugh, my husband says my son profits nothing in the world at his / book. I pray you ask him some questions in his accidence.
Sir Hugh, my husband says my son is learning nothing at all from his books. Please ask him some questions from his Latin grammar.
Come hither, William. Hold up your head, come.
Come here, William. Hold your head up; come.
Come on, sirrah. Hold up your head. Answer your master, be not afraid.
Come on, boy. Hold your head up. Answer your teacher; don't be afraid.
William, how many numbers is in nouns?
William, how many numbers are there in nouns?
Truly, I thought there had been one number more, because they say / "'Od's nouns."
Honestly, I thought there was one number more, because people say "God's nouns", I mean wounds.
Peace your tattlings! What is "fair," William?
Stop your chattering! What is the Latin for "fair", William?
Polecats? There are fairer things than polecats, sure.
Polecats? There are fairer things than polecats, surely.
You are a very simplicity 'oman; I pray you, peace.—What is lapis, / William?
You are a very simple woman; please be quiet. What is lapis, William?
No, it is lapis. I pray you remember in your prain.
No, it is lapis. Please remember that in your brain.
That is a good William. What is he, William, that does lend articles?
That's a good William. What is it, William, that lends articles?
Articles are borrowed of the pronoun, and be thus declined: / singulariter, nominativo, hic, haec, hoc.
Articles are borrowed from the pronoun, and are declined like this: singular, nominative, hic, haec, hoc.
Nominativo, hig, haeg, hog, pray you, mark: genitivo, huius. Well, / what is your accusative case?
Nominative, hig, haeg, hog; please note: genitive, huius. Well, what is your accusative case?
I pray you, have your remembrance, child. Accusativo, hung, hang, / hog.
Please use your memory, child. Accusative, hung, hang, hog.
"Hang-hog" is Latin for bacon, I warrant you.
"Hang-hog" is Latin for bacon, I bet.
Leave your prabbles, 'oman.—What is the focative case, William?
Stop your babbling, woman. What is the vocative case, William?
Remember, William; the vocative is caret, it is lacking.
And a carrot is a good root.
What is your genitive case plural, William?
What is your genitive case plural, William?
Vengeance of Jenny's case, fie on her! Never name her, child, if she be / a whore.
Curse Jenny's case, shame on her! Never mention her, child, if she's a whore.
You do ill to teach the child such words.—He teaches him to hick and to / hack, which they'll do fast enough of themselves; and to call "whore / 'm"!—Fie upon you!
You do wrong to teach the child such words. He's teaching him to hic and to hac, meaning drink and lechery, which they'll learn fast enough by themselves; and to say "whore 'em"! Shame on you!
'Oman, art thou lunatics? Hast thou no understandings for thy cases, / and the numbers of the genders? Thou art as foolish Christian creatures / as I would desires.
Woman, are you mad? Don't you understand cases, and the numbers of the genders? You are as foolish a Christian creature as anyone could wish.
Show me now, William, some declensions of your pronouns.
Now show me, William, some declensions of your pronouns.
It is qui, quae, quod. If you forget your quis, your quaes, and / your quods, you must be preeches. Go your ways and play, go.
It is qui, quae, quod. If you forget your quis, your quaes and your quods, you'll be getting your breeches down for a whipping. Off you go and play, go.
He is a better scholar than I thought he was.
He's a better scholar than I thought he was.
He is a good sprag memory. Farewell, Mistress Page.
He has a good quick memory. Goodbye, Mistress Page.
Get you home, boy. Come, we stay too long.
Go home, boy. Come, we've stayed too long.

Mistress Ford, your sorrow hath eaten up my sufferance. I see you are / obsequious in your love, and I profess requital to a hair's breadth, / not only, Mistress Ford, in the simple office of love, but in all the / accoutrement, compliment, and ceremony of it. But are you sure of your / husband now?

Mistress Ford, your sorrow has swallowed up my suffering. I can see you are devoted in your love, and I promise to repay it to a hair's breadth, Mistress Ford, not only in the simple act of love, but in all its trappings, compliments and ceremony. But are you sure of your husband now?
He's out bird hunting, sweet Sir John.
[Within] What ho, gossip Ford, what ho!
Step into the chamber, Sir John.
Step into the bedroom, Sir John.
How now, sweetheart, who's at home besides yourself?
Hello, sweetheart, who's at home apart from you?
Why, none but mine own people.
Why, nobody but my own servants.
No, certainly. / [Aside to her] Speak louder.
No, certainly. (Aside to her) Speak louder.
Truly, I am so glad you have nobody here.
Honestly, I'm so glad you have nobody here.

Why, woman, your husband is in his old lunes again. He so takes on / yonder with my husband, so rails against all married mankind, so curses / all Eve's daughters, of what complexion soever, and so buffets himself / on the forehead, crying "Peer out, peer out!" that any madness I ever / yet beheld seemed but tameness, civility, and patience, to this his / distemper he is in now. I am glad the fat knight is not here.

Why, woman, your husband is in one of his old fits of madness again. He's raving so to my husband over there, ranting so against all married men, cursing all Eve's daughters of whatever colouring, and beating himself on the forehead crying "Come out, come out!", that every madness I ever saw seems like tameness, good manners and patience compared to the fit he is in now. I'm glad the fat knight isn't here.
Why, does he talk of him?
Why, is he talking about him?

Of none but him, and swears he was carried out, the last time he / searched for him, in a basket; protests to my husband he is now here; / and hath drawn him and the rest of their company from their sport, to / make another experiment of his suspicion. But I am glad the knight is / not here. Now he shall see his own foolery.

About nobody but him; and he swears that the last time he searched for him, he was carried out in a basket. He insists to my husband that he's here now, and he has dragged him and the rest of their party away from their sport to test his suspicion again. But I'm glad the knight isn't here. Now he'll see his own foolishness.
How near is he, Mistress Page?
How close is he, Mistress Page?
Hard by, at street end. He will be here anon.
Close by, at the end of the street. He'll be here soon.
I am undone! The knight is here.
I'm ruined! The knight is here.
Why, then, you are utterly shamed, and he's but a dead man. What a / woman are you! Away with him, away with him! Better shame than murder.
Why, then you are completely disgraced, and he's a dead man. What a woman you are! Get him out, get him out! Better shame than murder.
Which way should he go? How should I bestow him? Shall I put him into / the basket again?
Which way should he go? Where should I put him? Shall I put him in the basket again?
No, I'll come no more i' the basket. May I not go out ere he come?
No, I won't go in the basket again. Can't I get out before he comes?
Alas, three of Master Ford's brothers watch the door with pistols, that / none shall issue out, otherwise you might slip away ere he came. But / what make you here?
Alas, three of Master Ford's brothers are guarding the door with pistols so that nobody can get out; otherwise you could slip away before he came. But what are you doing here?
What shall I do? I'll creep up into the chimney.
What shall I do? I'll climb up the chimney.
There they always use to discharge their birding-pieces.
That's where they always fire off their hunting guns.

He will seek there, on my word. Neither press, coffer, chest, trunk, / well, vault, but he hath an abstract for the remembrance of such / places, and goes to them by his note. There is no hiding you in the / house.

He'll look there, I promise you. There isn't a cupboard, coffer, chest, trunk, well or vault that he hasn't got on a list to remind him, and he goes to them by his notes. There's no hiding you in the house.
If you go out in your own semblance, you die, Sir John—unless you go / out disguised.
If you go out looking like yourself, you're dead, Sir John, unless you go out in disguise.
Alas the day, I know not. There is no woman's gown big enough for him; / otherwise he might put on a hat, a muffler, and a kerchief, and so / escape.
Oh dear, I don't know. There's no woman's dress big enough for him; otherwise he could put on a hat, a scarf and a headscarf, and escape that way.
Good hearts, devise something. Any extremity rather than a mischief.
Good hearts, think of something. Anything extreme rather than disaster.
My maid's aunt, the fat woman of Brentford, has a gown above.
My maid's aunt, the fat woman of Brentford, has a dress upstairs.
On my word, it will serve him. She's as big as he is. And there's her / thrummed hat, and her muffler too.—Run up, Sir John.
On my word, it will fit him. She's as big as he is. And there's her tufted hat and her scarf too. Run upstairs, Sir John.
Go, go, sweet Sir John. Mistress Page and I will look some linen for / your head.
Go, go, sweet Sir John. Mistress Page and I will find some linen for your head.
Quick, quick! We'll come dress you straight; put on the gown the while.
Quick, quick! We'll come and dress you straight away; put on the dress in the meantime.
I would my husband would meet him in this shape. He cannot abide the / old woman of Brentford; he swears she's a witch, forbade her my house, / and hath threatened to beat her.
I wish my husband would meet him dressed like that. He can't stand the old woman of Brentford; he swears she's a witch, has banned her from my house and has threatened to beat her.
Heaven guide him to thy husband's cudgel and the devil guide his cudgel / afterwards!
Heaven lead him to your husband's club, and the devil guide the club after that!
But is my husband really coming?
Ay, in good sadness is he, and talks of the basket too, howsoever he / hath had intelligence.
Yes, in all seriousness he is, and he's talking about the basket too, however he found out.
We'll try that; for I'll appoint my men to carry the basket again, to / meet him at the door with it as they did last time.
We'll test that, because I'll tell my men to carry the basket again and meet him at the door with it, as they did last time.
Nay, but he'll be here presently. Let's go dress him like the witch of / Brentford.
No, but he'll be here any minute. Let's go and dress him up as the witch of Brentford.
I'll first direct my men what they shall do with the basket. Go up, / I'll bring linen for him straight.
First I'll tell my men what to do with the basket. Go up; I'll bring linen for him straight away.

Hang him, dishonest varlet! We cannot misuse him enough. / We'll leave a proof, by that which we will do, / Wives may be merry and yet honest too. / We do not act that often jest and laugh; / 'Tis old but true: "Still swine eats all the draff."

Hang him, the lecherous rogue! We can't treat him badly enough. We'll prove, by what we do, that wives can be merry and still be faithful. We who often joke and laugh don't actually do it; the old saying is true: "The quiet pig eats all the swill."
