Go, sirs, take the basket again on your shoulders. Your master is hard / at door; if he bid you set it down, obey him. Quickly, dispatch.
Go on, men, lift the basket onto your shoulders again. Your master is nearly at the door; if he tells you to put it down, obey him. Quickly, hurry.
Come on, come on, pick it up.
Pray heaven it be not full of knight again.
Pray heaven it isn't full of knight again.
I hope not, I had lief as bear so much lead.
I hope not; I'd as soon carry the same weight in lead.

Ay, but if it prove true, Master Page, have you any way then to unfool / me again?—Set down the basket, villain! Somebody call my wife. Youth in / a basket! O you panderly rascals! There's a knot, a gin, a pack, a / conspiracy against me. Now shall the devil be shamed.—What, wife, I / say! Come, come forth! Behold what honest clothes you send forth to / bleaching!

Yes, but if it turns out to be true, Master Page, do you have any way of un-fooling me then? Put down the basket, villain! Somebody call my wife. A young lover in a basket! Oh, you pimping rascals! There's a gang, a trap, a pack, a conspiracy against me. Now the devil will be shamed. Wife, I say! Come, come out! Look what honest clothes you're sending out to be bleached!
Why, this passes, Master Ford! You are not to go loose any longer; you / must be pinioned.
Why, this goes too far, Master Ford! You can't be let loose any longer; you need to be tied up.
Why, this is lunatics, this is mad as a mad dog.
Why, this is lunacy; this is as mad as a mad dog.
Indeed, Master Ford, this is not well, indeed.
Really, Master Ford, this is not right, really.
Come hither, Mistress Ford—Mistress Ford, the honest woman, the modest / wife, the virtuous creature, that hath the jealous fool to her husband! / I suspect without cause, mistress, do I?
Come here, Mistress Ford. Mistress Ford, the honest woman, the modest wife, the virtuous creature, who has a jealous fool for a husband! I suspect without cause, madam, do I?
Heaven be my witness you do, if you suspect me in any dishonesty.
Heaven be my witness, you do, if you suspect me of any unfaithfulness.
Well said, brazen-face, hold it out.—Come forth, sirrah.
Well said, brazen face; keep it up. Come out, you rogue.
Are you not ashamed? Let the clothes alone.
Aren't you ashamed? Leave the clothes alone.
'Tis unreasonable. Will you take up your wife's clothes? Come, away.
It's unreasonable. Will you pick up your wife's clothes? Come away.

Master Page, as I am a man, there was one conveyed out of my house / yesterday in this basket. Why may not he be there again? In my house I / am sure he is. My intelligence is true, my jealousy is / reasonable.—Pluck me out all the linen.

Master Page, as I'm a man, someone was smuggled out of my house in this basket yesterday. Why couldn't he be in it again? I'm sure he's in my house. My information is true; my jealousy is reasonable. Pull out all the linen for me.
If you find a man there, he shall die a flea's death.
If you find a man there, he'll die like a flea.
By my fidelity, this is not well, Master Ford, this wrongs you.
On my word, this is not right, Master Ford; this does you wrong.
Master Ford, you must pray, and not follow the imaginations of your own / heart. This is jealousies.
Master Ford, you must pray, and not follow the fancies of your own heart. This is jealousy.
Well, he's not here I seek for.
Well, the man I'm looking for isn't here.
No, nor nowhere else but in your brain.
No, nor anywhere else but in your head.

Help to search my house this one time. If I find not what I seek, show / no colour for my extremity, let me for ever be your table-sport. Let / them say of me "As jealous as Ford, that searched a hollow walnut for / his wife's leman." Satisfy me once more, once more search with me.

Help me search my house this one time. If I don't find what I'm looking for, don't make any excuses for my extreme behaviour; let me be your joke at the dinner table for ever. Let them say of me, "As jealous as Ford, who searched a hollow walnut for his wife's lover." Satisfy me once more; search with me once more.
What, ho, Mistress Page! Come you and the old woman down; my husband / will come into the chamber.
Hello, Mistress Page! Come down, you and the old woman; my husband is coming into the bedroom.
Old woman? What old woman's that?
Old woman? What old woman is that?
Why, it is my maid's aunt of Brentford.
Why, it's my maid's aunt from Brentford.

A witch, a quean, an old cozening quean! Have I not forbid her my / house? She comes of errands, does she? We are simple men; we do not / know what's brought to pass under the profession of fortune-telling. / She works by charms, by spells, by the figure, and such daubery as this / is, beyond our element. We know nothing.—Come down, you witch, you hag, / you! Come down, I say!

A witch, a hussy, an old cheating hussy! Haven't I banned her from my house? She comes on errands, does she? We are simple men; we don't know what goes on under the pretence of fortune-telling. She works with charms, with spells, with astrological charts and that kind of trickery, beyond our understanding. We know nothing. Come down, you witch, you hag, you! Come down, I say!
Nay, good sweet husband!—Good gentlemen, let him not strike the old / woman.
No, good sweet husband! Good gentlemen, don't let him hit the old woman.
Come, Mother Prat; come, give me your hand.
Come, Mother Prat; come, give me your hand.
I'll prat her. [Beats him] Out of my door, you witch, you rag, you / baggage, you polecat, you runnion! Out, out! I'll conjure you, I'll / fortune-tell you.
I'll prat her. (Beats him) Out of my house, you witch, you rag, you slut, you polecat, you scab! Out, out! I'll cast a spell on you, I'll tell your fortune for you.
Are you not ashamed? I think you have killed the poor woman.
Aren't you ashamed? I think you've killed the poor woman.
Nay, he will do it. 'Tis a goodly credit for you.
Yes, he'll do it. It's a fine credit to you.
By yea and no, I think the 'oman is a witch indeed. I like not when a / 'oman has a great peard. I spy a great peard under her muffler.
Yes and no, I think the woman really is a witch. I don't like it when a woman has a big beard. I saw a big beard under her scarf.
Will you follow, gentlemen? I beseech you follow, see but the issue of / my jealousy. If I cry out thus upon no trail, never trust me when I / open again.
Will you follow me, gentlemen? I beg you to follow; just see how my jealousy turns out. If I bark like this on no scent, never trust me when I give tongue again.
Let's obey his humour a little further. Come, gentlemen.
Let's humour his mood a little longer. Come, gentlemen.
Trust me, he beat him most pitifully.
Honestly, he beat him most pitifully.
Nay, by th' mass, that he did not; he beat him most unpitifully, / methought.
No, by the Mass, he didn't; he beat him most pitilessly, I thought.
I'll have the cudgel hallowed and hung o'er the altar. It hath done / meritorious service.
I'll have the club blessed and hung over the altar. It has done praiseworthy service.
What think you? May we, with the warrant of womanhood and the witness / of a good conscience, pursue him with any further revenge?
What do you think? Can we, with a woman's right and a clear conscience, pursue him with any more revenge?
The spirit of wantonness is sure scared out of him. If the devil have / him not in fee-simple, with fine and recovery, he will never, I think, / in the way of waste, attempt us again.
The spirit of lechery has surely been frightened out of him. Unless the devil owns him outright, by every legal title, I don't think he will ever try to ruin us again.
Shall we tell our husbands how we have served him?
Shall we tell our husbands how we've treated him?

Yes, by all means, if it be but to scrape the figures out of your / husband's brains. If they can find in their hearts the poor unvirtuous / fat knight shall be any further afflicted, we two will still be the / ministers.

Yes, by all means, if only to scrape the fantasies out of your husband's brain. If they can find it in their hearts to have the poor sinful fat knight punished any further, we two will still carry it out.
I'll warrant they'll have him publicly shamed, and methinks there would / be no period to the jest should he not be publicly shamed.
I bet they'll want him publicly shamed, and I think the joke won't be complete unless he is publicly shamed.
Come, to the forge with it, then shape it. I would not have things / cool.
Come, to the forge with it, then, and hammer it into shape. I don't want things to cool off.
Sir, the Germans desire to have three of your horses. The Duke himself / will be tomorrow at court, and they are going to meet him.
Sir, the Germans want three of your horses. The Duke himself will be at court tomorrow, and they are going to meet him.
What duke should that be comes so secretly? I hear not of him in the / court. Let me speak with the gentlemen. They speak English?
What duke could that be who comes so secretly? I've heard nothing of him at court. Let me speak to the gentlemen. Do they speak English?
Ay, sir. I'll call them to you.
Yes, sir. I'll call them for you.
They shall have my horses, but I'll make them pay, I'll sauce them. / They have had my house a week at command; I have turned away my other / guests. They must come off, I'll sauce them. Come.

They can have my horses, but I'll make them pay; I'll overcharge them. They've had my house at their command for a week; I've turned away my other guests. They'll have to pay up; I'll overcharge them. Come.
'Tis one of the best discretions of a 'oman as ever I did look upon.
It is one of the most sensible things a woman ever did that I have seen.
And did he send you both these letters at an instant?
And did he send you both these letters at the same moment?
Within a quarter of an hour.
Within a quarter of an hour.

Pardon me, wife. Henceforth, do what thou wilt. / I rather will suspect the sun with cold / Than thee with wantonness. Now doth thy honour stand, / In him that was of late an heretic, / As firm as faith.
Forgive me, wife. From now on, do what you like. I'd sooner suspect the sun of being cold than you of being unfaithful. Now your honour stands as firm as faith in a man who was lately a heretic.

'Tis well, 'tis well, no more. / Be not as extreme in submission as in offence. / But let our plot go forward. Let our wives / Yet once again, to make us public sport, / Appoint a meeting with this old fat fellow, / Where we may take him and disgrace him for it.

That's fine, that's fine, no more. Don't be as extreme in your apology as you were in your offence. But let our plot go ahead. Let our wives, once more, to give us public fun, arrange a meeting with this fat old fellow, where we can catch him and disgrace him for it.
There is no better way than that they spoke of.
There's no better way than the one they described.
How? To send him word they'll meet him in the park at midnight? Fie, / fie, he'll never come.
What? To send him word that they'll meet him in the park at midnight? No, no, he'll never come.

You say he has been thrown in the rivers, and has been grievously / peaten as an old 'oman. Methinks there should be terrors in him, that / he should not come. Methinks his flesh is punished; he shall have no / desires.
You say he has been thrown in the river and badly beaten as an old woman. I think he must be terrified, so he won't come. I think his flesh has been punished; he won't have any desires.
Devise but how you'll use him when he comes, / And let us two devise to bring him thither.
You just work out how you'll treat him when he comes, and let us two work out how to get him there.

There is an old tale goes that Herne the hunter, / Sometime a keeper here in Windsor Forest, / Doth all the winter time, at still midnight, / Walk round about an oak, with great ragged horns, / And there he blasts the tree, and takes the cattle, / And makes milch-kine yield blood, and shakes a chain / In a most hideous and dreadful manner. / You have heard of such a spirit, and well you know / The superstitious idle-headed eld / Received and did deliver to our age, / This tale of Herne the hunter for a truth.

There is an old story that Herne the hunter, once a keeper here in Windsor Forest, walks round an oak tree all winter at dead of midnight, with great ragged horns; and there he withers the tree, bewitches the cattle, makes milking cows give blood, and rattles a chain in a hideous and dreadful way. You have heard of such a spirit, and you know well that superstitious, foolish old people accepted this tale of Herne the hunter as true and handed it down to our times.
Why, yet there want not many that do fear / In deep of night to walk by this Herne's oak. / But what of this?
Why, there are still plenty of people who are afraid to walk by this Herne's oak in the dead of night. But what about it?
Marry, this is our device, / That Falstaff at that oak shall meet with us, / Disguised like Herne, with huge horns on his head.
Well, this is our plan: that Falstaff will meet us at that oak, disguised as Herne, with huge horns on his head.
Well, let it not be doubted but he'll come, / And in this shape; when you have brought him thither, / What shall be done with him? What is your plot?
Well, don't doubt that he'll come, and in that disguise. When you've got him there, what shall be done with him? What's your plan?

That likewise have we thought upon, and thus: / Nan Page my daughter, and my little son, / And three or four more of their growth, we'll dress / Like urchins, oafs and fairies, green and white, / With rounds of waxen tapers on their heads / And rattles in their hands. Upon a sudden, / As Falstaff, she, and I are newly met, / Let them from forth a sawpit rush at once / With some diffused song; upon their sight / We two in great amazedness will fly. / Then let them all encircle him about, / And fairy-like, to pinch the unclean knight, / And ask him why, that hour of fairy revel, / In their so sacred paths he dares to tread / In shape profane.

We've thought about that too, and this is it: we'll dress my daughter Nan Page, my little son, and three or four more of their size as goblins, elves and fairies in green and white, with circles of wax candles on their heads and rattles in their hands. Suddenly, just as Falstaff, she and I have met, let them all rush out together from a sawpit, singing some wild song. When we see them, we two will run off in great alarm. Then let them all make a circle round him and, like fairies, pinch the filthy knight, and ask him why, at the hour of the fairies' revels, he dares to tread their sacred paths in such an unholy shape.
And till he tell the truth, / Let the supposed fairies pinch him sound / And burn him with their tapers.
And until he tells the truth, let the pretend fairies pinch him hard and burn him with their candles.
The truth being known, / We'll all present ourselves, dis-horn the spirit, / And mock him home to Windsor.
When the truth is out, we'll all show ourselves, take the spirit's horns off and mock him all the way home to Windsor.
The children must / Be practised well to this, or they'll ne'er do 't.
The children must be well rehearsed for this, or they'll never manage it.
I will teach the children their behaviours, and I will be like a / jackanapes also, to burn the knight with my taber.
I will teach the children how to behave, and I will dress like a monkey too, to burn the knight with my taper.
That will be excellent. I'll go buy them vizards.
That will be excellent. I'll go and buy them masks.
My Nan shall be the queen of all the fairies, / Finely attired in a robe of white.
My Nan shall be the queen of all the fairies, beautifully dressed in a white robe.
That silk will I go buy. / [Aside] And in that time / Shall Master Slender steal my Nan away, / And marry her at Eton.—Go, send to Falstaff straight.
I'll go and buy the silk. (Aside) And in that time Master Slender will steal my Nan away and marry her at Eton. Go, send to Falstaff at once.
Nay, I'll to him again in name of Brook. / He'll tell me all his purpose. Sure, he'll come.
No, I'll go to him again as Brook. He'll tell me all his plans. He'll certainly come.
Fear not you that. Go, get us properties / And tricking for our fairies.
Don't you worry about that. Go and get us props and costumes for our fairies.
Let us about it. It is admirable pleasures and fery honest knaveries.
Let's get on with it. It is wonderful fun and very honest mischief.
Go, Mistress Ford. / Send quickly to Sir John to know his mind.
Go, Mistress Ford. Send quickly to Sir John to find out what he thinks.

I'll to the Doctor. He hath my good will, / And none but he, to marry with Nan Page. / That Slender, though well landed, is an idiot, / And he my husband best of all affects. / The Doctor is well moneyed, and his friends / Potent at court. He, none but he, shall have her, / Though twenty thousand worthier come to crave her.

I'll go to the Doctor. He has my blessing, and no one but him, to marry Nan Page. That Slender, though he owns plenty of land, is an idiot, and my husband prefers him above all. The Doctor has plenty of money, and his friends are powerful at court. He, and no one else, shall have her, even if twenty thousand worthier men come to ask for her.
What wouldst thou have, boor? What, thick-skin? Speak, breathe, / discuss; brief, short, quick, snap.
What do you want, peasant? Well, thick-skull? Speak, breathe, explain; brief, short, quick, snap.
Marry, sir, I come to speak with Sir John Falstaff from Master Slender.
Well, sir, I've come to speak with Sir John Falstaff on behalf of Master Slender.

There's his chamber, his house, his castle, his standing-bed and / truckle-bed. 'Tis painted about with the story of the Prodigal, fresh / and new. Go, knock and call. He'll speak like an Anthropophaginian unto / thee. Knock, I say.

There's his room, his house, his castle, his four-poster bed and his trundle bed. It's painted all round with the story of the Prodigal Son, fresh and new. Go, knock and call. He'll speak to you like a cannibal. Knock, I say.
There's an old woman, a fat woman, gone up into his chamber. I'll be so / bold as stay, sir, till she come down. I come to speak with her, / indeed.
There's an old woman, a fat woman, gone up into his room. I'll make so bold as to wait, sir, until she comes down. It's really her I've come to speak to.
Ha? A fat woman? The knight may be robbed. I'll call.—Bully knight! / Bully Sir John! Speak from thy lungs military. Art thou there? It is / thine host, thine Ephesian, calls.

What? A fat woman? The knight might be robbed. I'll call. My fine knight! My fine Sir John! Speak up from your soldier's lungs. Are you there? It's your landlord, your good drinking companion, calling.
Here's a Bohemian-Tartar tarries the coming down of thy fat woman. Let / her descend, bully, let her descend. My chambers are honourable. Fie! / Privacy? Fie!
Here's a wild foreigner waiting for your fat woman to come down. Let her come down, my lad, let her come down. My rooms are respectable. Shame! Private meetings? Shame!
There was, mine host, an old fat woman even now with me, but she's / gone.
Landlord, there was an old fat woman with me just now, but she's gone.
Pray you, sir, was't not the wise woman of Brentford?
Please, sir, wasn't it the wise woman of Brentford?
Ay, marry was it, mussel-shell. What would you with her?
Yes, it was indeed, mussel-shell. What do you want with her?
My master, sir, my Master Slender, sent to her, seeing her go through / the streets, to know, sir, whether one Nym, sir, that beguiled him of a / chain, had the chain or no.
My master, sir, my Master Slender, seeing her go through the streets, sent me to her to find out, sir, whether a man called Nym, sir, who cheated him of a chain, had the chain or not.
I spake with the old woman about it.
I talked to the old woman about it.
And what says she, I pray, sir?
And what does she say, please, sir?
Marry, she says that the very same man that beguiled Master Slender of / his chain cozened him of it.
Well, she says that the very same man who cheated Master Slender of his chain swindled him out of it.
I would I could have spoken with the woman herself. I had other things / to have spoken with her too, from him.
I wish I could have spoken to the woman herself. I had other things to ask her too, from him.
What are they? Let us know.
What are they? Let's hear them.
I may not conceal them, sir.
I mayn't conceal them, I mean reveal them, sir.
Why, sir, they were nothing but about Mistress Anne Page, to know if it / were my master's fortune to have her or no.
Well, sir, they were only about Mistress Anne Page, to find out whether my master is fated to have her or not.
It is, it is his fate.
To have her, or no. Go, say the woman told me so.
To have her, or not. Go and say the woman told me so.
May I be bold to say so, sir?
May I be so bold as to say so, sir?
Ay, sir; like who more bold?
Yes, sir; who could be bolder?
I thank your worship; I shall make my master glad with these tidings.
Thank you, your worship; I'll make my master happy with this news.
Thou art clerkly, thou art clerkly, Sir John. Was there a wise woman / with thee?
You're clever, you're clever, Sir John. Was there really a wise woman with you?
Ay, that there was, mine host; one that hath taught me more wit than / ever I learned before in my life; and I paid nothing for it neither, / but was paid for my learning.
Yes, there was, landlord; one who has taught me more sense than I ever learned before in my life; and I didn't pay anything for it either, but was paid for my lesson.
Out, alas, sir, cozenage, mere cozenage!
Oh no, sir, a swindle, a complete swindle!
Where be my horses? Speak well of them, varletto.
Where are my horses? Give me good news of them, you rascal.

Run away, with the cozeners. For so soon as I came beyond Eton, they / threw me off from behind one of them, in a slough of mire, and set / spurs and away, like three German devils, three Doctor Faustuses.
Run off with the swindlers. As soon as we got past Eton, they threw me off from behind one of them into a muddy bog, and spurred off like three German devils, three Doctor Faustuses.
They are gone but to meet the Duke, villain, do not say they be fled. / Germans are honest men.
They've only gone to meet the Duke, villain; don't say they've run off. Germans are honest men.

Have a care of your entertainments. There is a friend of mine come to / town tells me there is three cozen-Germans that has cozened all the / hosts of Readings, of Maidenhead, of Colebrook, of horses and money. I / tell you for good will, look you. You are wise, and full of gibes and / vlouting-stocks, and 'tis not convenient you should be cozened. Fare / you well.

Be careful who you take in. A friend of mine who has come to town tells me there are three cheating cousin-Germans who have swindled all the innkeepers of Reading, Maidenhead and Colnbrook out of horses and money. I tell you this out of goodwill, you see. You are clever, full of jokes and mockery, and it wouldn't be fitting for you to be swindled. Goodbye.
Vere is mine host de Jarteer?
Where is my landlord of the Garter?
Here, Master Doctor, in perplexity and doubtful dilemma.
Here, Doctor, in a state of confusion and uncertain dilemma.
I cannot tell vat is dat, but it is tell-a me dat you make grand / preparation for a Duke de Jamany. By my trot, dere is no duke that the / court is know to come. I tell you for good will. Adieu.
I don't know what that is, but I am told that you are making great preparations for a Duke of Germany. On my word, the court knows of no duke who is coming. I tell you out of goodwill. Goodbye.
Hue and cry, villain, go!—Assist me, knight, I am undone.—Fly, run, hue / and cry, villain, I am undone!
Raise the alarm, villain, go! Help me, knight; I'm ruined. Hurry, run, raise the alarm, villain; I'm ruined!

I would all the world might be cozened, for I have been cozened and / beaten too. If it should come to the ear of the court how I have been / transformed, and how my transformation hath been washed and cudgelled, / they would melt me out of my fat drop by drop, and liquor fishermen's / boots with me. I warrant they would whip me with their fine wits till I / were as crestfallen as a dried pear. I never prospered since I forswore / myself at primero. Well, if my wind were but long enough, I would / repent.

I wish the whole world could be swindled, because I've been swindled and beaten too. If the court ever heard how I've been transformed, and how my transformation has been washed and clubbed, they would melt the fat out of me drop by drop and grease fishermen's boots with me. I bet they'd whip me with their sharp wit until I was as shrivelled as a dried pear. I've never had any luck since I cheated at cards. Well, if I had breath enough, I would repent.
Now, where have you come from?

The devil take one party and his dam the other, and so they shall be / both bestowed. I have suffered more for their sakes, more than the / villainous inconstancy of man's disposition is able to bear.
The devil take one party and his mother the other, and then both will be taken care of. I have suffered more for their sakes than the wretched weakness of man's nature can bear.
And have not they suffered? Yes, I warrant, speciously one of them. / Mistress Ford, good heart, is beaten black and blue, that you cannot / see a white spot about her.
And haven't they suffered? Yes, I promise you, especially one of them. Mistress Ford, poor heart, has been beaten black and blue, so you can't see a white spot on her.

What tellst thou me of black and blue? I was beaten myself into all the / colours of the rainbow, and was like to be apprehended for the witch of / Brentford. But that my admirable dexterity of wit, my counterfeiting / the action of an old woman, delivered me, the knave constable had set / me i' the stocks, i' the common stocks, for a witch.

Why are you telling me about black and blue? I was beaten myself into all the colours of the rainbow, and nearly arrested as the witch of Brentford. If my wonderful quick wits, my imitation of the way an old woman walks, hadn't saved me, that rogue of a constable would have put me in the stocks, the public stocks, as a witch.

Sir, let me speak with you in your chamber, you shall hear how things / go, and, I warrant, to your content. Here is a letter will say / somewhat. Good hearts, what ado here is to bring you together! Sure, / one of you does not serve heaven well, that you are so crossed.

Sir, let me talk to you in your room; you'll hear how things stand, and to your satisfaction, I promise. Here is a letter that will tell you something. Goodness, what trouble there is in bringing you together! Surely one of you isn't serving heaven well, since you are so thwarted.
Master Fenton, talk not to me. My mind is heavy. I will give over all.
Master Fenton, don't talk to me. My mind is heavy. I'll give up everything.
Yet hear me speak. Assist me in my purpose, / And, as I am a gentleman, I'll give thee / A hundred pound in gold more than your loss.
But hear me out. Help me with my plan, and as I am a gentleman, I'll give you a hundred pounds in gold on top of what you've lost.
I will hear you, Master Fenton, and I will, at the least, keep your / counsel.
I'll hear you, Master Fenton, and at the very least I'll keep your secret.

From time to time I have acquainted you / With the dear love I bear to fair Anne Page, / Who mutually hath answered my affection, / So far forth as herself might be her chooser, / Even to my wish. I have a letter from her / Of such contents as you will wonder at, / The mirth whereof so larded with my matter / That neither singly can be manifested / Without the show of both, wherein fat Falstaff / Hath a great scene; the image of the jest / I'll show you here at large. Hark, good mine host: / Tonight at Herne's oak, just 'twixt twelve and one, / Must my sweet Nan present the Fairy Queen— / The purpose why is here—in which disguise, / While other jests are something rank on foot, / Her father hath commanded her to slip / Away with Slender, and with him at Eton / Immediately to marry. She hath consented. Now, sir, / Her mother, even strong against that match / And firm for Doctor Caius, hath appointed / That he shall likewise shuffle her away, / While other sports are tasking of their minds, / And at the dean'ry, where a priest attends, / Straight marry her. To this her mother's plot / She, seemingly obedient, likewise hath / Made promise to the doctor. Now thus it rests: / Her father means she shall be all in white / And in that habit, when Slender sees his time / To take her by the hand and bid her go, / She shall go with him. Her mother hath intended / The better to denote her to the doctor, / For they must all be masked and vizarded— / That quaint in green she shall be loose enrobed, / With ribbons pendant flaring 'bout her head; / And when the doctor spies his vantage ripe, / To pinch her by the hand, and on that token / The maid hath given consent to go with him.

From time to time I have told you about my deep love for lovely Anne Page, who has returned my affection as fully as I could wish, as far as she is free to choose for herself. I have a letter from her with contents that will amaze you. The fun of it is so mixed up with my own business that neither can be explained without the other, and fat Falstaff has a big part in it. I'll show you the whole outline of the joke. Listen, good landlord. Tonight at Herne's oak, between twelve and one, my sweet Nan is to play the Fairy Queen (the reason is in here). In that disguise, while the other jokes are in full swing, her father has ordered her to slip away with Slender and marry him straight away at Eton. She has agreed. Now, sir, her mother, who is firmly against that match and set on Doctor Caius, has arranged that he will also spirit her away while the others are busy with their sport, and marry her at once at the deanery, where a priest will be waiting. To this plan of her mother's, she, seeming obedient, has also given her promise to the doctor. So this is how it stands. Her father means her to be dressed all in white, and in that costume, when Slender sees his chance to take her by the hand and tell her to come, she will go with him. Her mother intends, to mark her out better for the doctor (since they must all be masked and disguised), that she will be dressed loosely and prettily in green, with ribbons streaming round her head; and when the doctor sees his moment, he is to squeeze her hand, and at that signal the girl has agreed to go with him.
Which means she to deceive, father or mother?
Which one does she mean to deceive, her father or her mother?

Both, my good host, to go along with me. / And here it rests, that you'll procure the vicar / To stay for me at church, 'twixt twelve and one, / And, in the lawful name of marrying, / To give our hearts united ceremony.

Both, my good landlord, by going off with me. And this is where you come in: get the vicar to wait for me at the church between twelve and one and, in the lawful name of marriage, give our united hearts their ceremony.
Well, husband your device; I'll to the vicar. / Bring you the maid, you shall not lack a priest.
Well, manage your plan; I'll go to the vicar. You bring the girl, and you won't lack a priest.
So shall I evermore be bound to thee; / Besides, I'll make a present recompense.
Then I'll be in your debt for ever; and besides, I'll pay you something right away.

Prithee, no more prattling. Go. I'll hold. This is the third time; I / hope good luck lies in odd numbers. Away, go! They say there is / divinity in odd numbers, either in nativity, chance, or death. Away!

Please, no more chatter. Go. I'll keep the appointment. This is the third time; I hope there's good luck in odd numbers. Off you go! They say there is something divine in odd numbers, whether in birth, chance or death. Off!
I'll provide you a chain, and I'll do what I can to get you a pair of / horns.
I'll get you a chain, and I'll do what I can to get you a pair of horns.
Away, I say; time wears. Hold up your head, and mince.
Off, I say; time is passing. Hold your head up, and trip along.
How now, Master Brook! Master Brook, the matter will be known tonight / or never. Be you in the park about midnight, at Herne's oak, and you / shall see wonders.
Hello, Master Brook! Master Brook, it will be settled tonight or never. Be in the park around midnight, at Herne's oak, and you will see wonders.
Went you not to her yesterday, sir, as you told me you had appointed?
Didn't you go to her yesterday, sir, as you told me you had arranged?

I went to her, Master Brook, as you see, like a poor old man, but I / came from her, Master Brook, like a poor old woman. That same knave / Ford, her husband, hath the finest mad devil of jealousy in him, Master / Brook, that ever governed frenzy. I will tell you he beat me / grievously, in the shape of a woman; for in the shape of man, Master / Brook, I fear not Goliath with a weaver's beam, because I know also / life is a shuttle. I am in haste. Go along with me; I'll tell you all, / Master Brook. Since I plucked geese, played truant, and whipped top, I / knew not what 'twas to be beaten till lately. Follow me, I'll tell you / strange things of this knave Ford, on whom tonight I will be revenged, / and I will deliver his wife into your hand. Follow. Strange things in / hand, Master Brook! Follow.

I went to her, Master Brook, as you see me, like a poor old man; but I came away from her, Master Brook, like a poor old woman. That rogue Ford, her husband, has the finest mad devil of jealousy in him, Master Brook, that ever ruled a frenzy. I tell you, he beat me badly while I was dressed as a woman; because as a man, Master Brook, I wouldn't be afraid of Goliath with his spear like a weaver's beam, since I also know that life is as quick as a weaver's shuttle. I'm in a hurry. Come with me; I'll tell you everything, Master Brook. Since I was a boy plucking geese, playing truant and whipping tops, I never knew what it was to be beaten until lately. Follow me; I'll tell you strange things about this rogue Ford, on whom I'll have my revenge tonight, and I'll hand his wife over to you. Follow me. Strange things are afoot, Master Brook! Follow.
Come, come. We'll couch i' the castle ditch till we see the light of / our fairies. Remember, son Slender, my daughter—
Come, come. We'll hide in the castle ditch until we see the light of our fairies. Remember, son Slender, my daughter—
Ay, forsooth. I have spoke with her, and we have a nay-word how to know / one another. I come to her in white and cry "mum"; she cries "budget"; / and by that we know one another.
Yes, truly. I've spoken with her, and we have a password to recognise each other. I come to her in white and say "mum"; she says "budget"; and by that we know each other.
That's good too. But what needs either your "mum" or her "budget"? The / white will decipher her well enough. It hath struck ten o'clock.
That's good too. But what need is there for your "mum" or her "budget"? The white will identify her well enough. It has struck ten o'clock.
The night is dark. Light and spirits will become it well. Heaven / prosper our sport! No man means evil but the devil, and we shall know / him by his horns. Let's away; follow me.
The night is dark. Lights and spirits will suit it well. Heaven make our fun succeed! No one means harm except the devil, and we'll know him by his horns. Let's go; follow me.
Master Doctor, my daughter is in green. When you see your time, take / her by the hand, away with her to the deanery, and dispatch it quickly. / Go before into the park. We two must go together.
Doctor, my daughter is in green. When you see your chance, take her by the hand, off with her to the deanery and get it done quickly. Go ahead into the park. We two must go together.
I know vat I have to do. Adieu.
I know what I have to do. Goodbye.
My husband will not rejoice so much at the abuse of Falstaff as he will / chafe at the doctor's marrying my daughter. But 'tis no matter. Better / a little chiding than a great deal of heartbreak.
My husband won't be as pleased at the trick on Falstaff as he'll be angry at the doctor marrying my daughter. But it doesn't matter. Better a little scolding than a great deal of heartbreak.
Where is Nan now, and her troop of fairies, and the Welsh devil Hugh?
Where are Nan and her troop of fairies now, and that Welsh devil Hugh?
They are all couched in a pit hard by Herne's oak, with obscured / lights, which, at the very instant of Falstaff's and our meeting, they / will at once display to the night.
They're all hiding in a pit close to Herne's oak with their lights covered, and at the very moment Falstaff meets us, they will suddenly reveal them to the night.
That cannot choose but amaze him.
If he be not amazed, he will be mocked; if he be amazed, he will every / way be mocked.
If he isn't terrified, he'll be mocked; if he is terrified, he'll be mocked all the more.
Against such lewdsters and their lechery, / Those that betray them do no treachery.
Against such lechers and their lechery, those who trap them commit no treachery.
The hour draws on. To the oak, to the oak!
The hour is coming. To the oak, to the oak!
Trib, trib, fairies. Come, and remember your parts. Be pold, I pray / you, follow me into the pit, and when I give the watch-'ords, do as I / pid you. Come, come; trib, trib.
Trip, trip, fairies. Come, and remember your parts. Be bold, please; follow me into the pit, and when I give the password, do as I told you. Come, come; trip, trip.

The Windsor bell hath struck twelve, the minute draws on. Now the / hot-blooded gods assist me! Remember, Jove, thou wast a bull for thy / Europa; love set on thy horns. O powerful love, that in some respects, / makes a beast a man, in some other a man a beast! You were also, / Jupiter, a swan for the love of Leda. O omnipotent love, how near the / god drew to the complexion of a goose! A fault done first in the form / of a beast; O Jove, a beastly fault! And then another fault in the / semblance of a fowl; think on't, Jove, a foul fault! When gods have hot / backs, what shall poor men do? For me, I am here a Windsor stag, and / the fattest, I think, i' the forest. Send me a cool rut-time, Jove, or / who can blame me to piss my tallow? Who comes here? My doe?

The Windsor bell has struck twelve; the moment is coming. Now may the hot-blooded gods help me! Remember, Jove, you became a bull for your Europa; love gave you horns. Oh, powerful love, which in some ways turns a beast into a man, and in others a man into a beast! You were also a swan, Jupiter, for love of Leda. Oh, all-powerful love, how close the god came to looking like a goose! A sin committed first in the shape of a beast, oh Jove, a beastly sin! And then another sin in the shape of a bird; think about it, Jove, a fowl sin! When gods are on heat, what are poor men to do? As for me, here I am, a Windsor stag, and the fattest in the forest, I think. Send me a cool mating season, Jove, or who can blame me for sweating off my fat? Who's coming? My doe?
Sir John? Art thou there, my deer, my male deer?
Sir John? Are you there, my deer, my male deer?

My doe with the black scut! Let the sky rain potatoes, let it thunder / to the tune of "Greensleeves", hail kissing-comfits and snow eringoes; / let there come a tempest of provocation, I will shelter me here.

My doe with the black tail! Let the sky rain sweet potatoes, let it thunder to the tune of "Greensleeves", let it hail kissing sweets and snow aphrodisiacs; let a whole storm of temptation come, I'll shelter here.
Mistress Page is come with me, sweetheart.
Mistress Page has come with me, sweetheart.

Divide me like a bribed buck, each a haunch. I will keep my sides to / myself, my shoulders for the fellow of this walk, and my horns I / bequeath your husbands. Am I a woodman, ha? Speak I like Herne the / hunter? Why, now is Cupid a child of conscience; he makes restitution. / As I am a true spirit, welcome!

Divide me like a stolen deer, a haunch each. I'll keep my ribs for myself, my shoulders for the keeper of this part of the forest, and my horns I leave to your husbands. Am I a huntsman, ha? Do I speak like Herne the hunter? Why, now Cupid is a child with a conscience; he is making up for things. As I am a true spirit, welcome!
I think the devil will not have me damned, lest the oil that's in me / should set hell on fire; he would never else cross me thus.
I think the devil doesn't want me damned, in case the fat in me sets hell on fire; otherwise he would never thwart me like this.

Fairies, black, grey, green, and white, / You moonshine revellers and shades of night, / You orphan heirs of fixed destiny, / Attend your office and your quality. / Crier Hobgoblin, make the fairy oyes.

Fairies, black, grey, green and white, you moonlight revellers and shadows of the night, you orphaned children of unchanging fate, do your duty and your work. Hobgoblin, as crier, call the fairies to order.

Elves, list your names; silence, you airy toys! / Cricket, to Windsor chimneys shalt thou leap, / Where fires thou find'st unraked and hearths unswept, / There pinch the maids as blue as bilberry. / Our radiant queen hates sluts and sluttery.

Elves, listen for your names; silence, you airy creatures! Cricket, you will leap to Windsor's chimneys, and where you find fires not banked down and hearths not swept, pinch the maids there as blue as bilberries. Our radiant queen hates sluts and slovenliness.
They are fairies, he that speaks to them shall die. / I'll wink and couch. No man their works must eye.
They are fairies; whoever speaks to them will die. I'll shut my eyes and lie down. No man may watch what they do.

Where's Bead? Go you, and where you find a maid / That ere she sleep has thrice her prayers said, / Rein up the organs of her fantasy; / Sleep she as sound as careless infancy. / But those as sleep and think not on their sins, / Pinch them, arms, legs, backs, shoulders, sides, and shins.

Where's Bead? Go, and where you find a girl who has said her prayers three times before she sleeps, calm her imagination so she sleeps as soundly as a carefree baby. But those who sleep without thinking about their sins, pinch them on their arms, legs, backs, shoulders, sides and shins.

About, about! / Search Windsor castle, elves, within and out. / Strew good luck, oafs, on every sacred room, / That it may stand till the perpetual doom / In state as wholesome as in state 'tis fit, / Worthy the owner and the owner it. / The several chairs of order look you scour / With juice of balm and every precious flower. / Each fair instalment, coat, and several crest, / With loyal blazon, evermore be blest! / And nightly, meadow-fairies, look you sing, / Like to the Garter's compass, in a ring. / Th' expressure that it bears, green let it be, / More fertile-fresh than all the field to see; / And Honi soit qui mal y pense write / In em'rald tufts, flowers purple, blue and white, / Like sapphire, pearl, and rich embroidery, / Buckled below fair knighthood's bending knee. / Fairies use flowers for their charactery. / Away, disperse! But till 'tis one o'clock, / Our dance of custom round about the oak / Of Herne the hunter let us not forget.

Off you go, off you go! Search Windsor Castle, elves, inside and out. Scatter good luck, goblins, in every sacred room, so that it may stand until Judgement Day in a condition as sound as it is fitting, worthy of its owner and its owner worthy of it. Make sure you polish the stalls of the Order with balm and every precious flower. May every fair stall, coat of arms and crest, with its loyal emblem, be blessed for ever! And every night, meadow fairies, make sure you sing in a ring like the circle of the Garter. Let the mark it leaves in the grass be green, fresher and more fertile than the whole field around; and write "Honi soit qui mal y pense", the Garter's motto, in emerald tufts and purple, blue and white flowers, like sapphires, pearls and rich embroidery fastened below the bending knee of noble knighthood. Fairies use flowers for their writing. Away, scatter! But until one o'clock let us not forget our customary dance around the oak of Herne the hunter.
Pray you, lock hand in hand, yourselves in order set; / And twenty glow-worms shall our lanterns be, / To guide our measure round about the tree. / But stay, I smell a man of middle earth.
Please join hands, and put yourselves in order; and twenty glow-worms will be our lanterns to guide our dance round the tree. But wait, I smell a mortal man.
Heavens defend me from that Welsh fairy, lest he transform me to a / piece of cheese!
Heaven protect me from that Welsh fairy, in case he turns me into a piece of cheese!
Vile worm, thou wast o'erlooked even in thy birth.
Vile worm, you were bewitched from the moment you were born.
With trial-fire touch me his finger-end. / If he be chaste, the flame will back descend / And turn him to no pain; but if he start, / It is the flesh of a corrupted heart.
Touch the tip of his finger with the testing fire. If he is chaste, the flame will turn back and cause him no pain; but if he flinches, it is the flesh of a corrupt heart.
Come, will this wood take fire?
Come, will this wood catch fire?
Corrupt, corrupt, and tainted in desire! / About him, fairies, sing a scornful rhyme, / And, as you trip, still pinch him to your time.
Corrupt, corrupt and tainted with desire! Circle round him, fairies, sing a scornful rhyme, and as you dance, keep pinching him in time.

Fie on sinful fantasy! / Fie on lust and luxury! / Lust is but a bloody fire, / Kindled with unchaste desire, / Fed in heart, whose flames aspire, / As thoughts do blow them, higher and higher. / Pinch him, fairies, mutually; / Pinch him for his villainy. / Pinch him and burn him and turn him about, / Till candles and starlight and moonshine be out.

Shame on sinful fancies! Shame on lust and lechery! Lust is just a bloody fire, kindled by unchaste desire, fed in the heart, whose flames rise as thoughts blow on them, higher and higher. Pinch him, fairies, all together; pinch him for his villainy. Pinch him and burn him and turn him about, till candles and starlight and moonlight are out.
Nay, do not fly. I think we have watched you now. / Will none but Herne the hunter serve your turn?
No, don't run away. I think we've caught you now. Will nothing but Herne the hunter do for you?
I pray you, come, hold up the jest no higher.— / Now, good Sir John, how like you Windsor wives? / See you these, husband?
Please, come, don't push the joke any further. Now, good Sir John, how do you like Windsor wives? Do you see these, husband?
Do not these fair yokes / Become the forest better than the town?
Don't these fine horns suit the forest better than the town?

Now, sir, who's a cuckold now? Master Brook, Falstaff's a knave, a / cuckoldly knave. Here are his horns, Master Brook. And, Master Brook, / he hath enjoyed nothing of Ford's but his buck-basket, his cudgel, and / twenty pounds of money, which must be paid to Master Brook. His horses / are arrested for it, Master Brook.

Now, sir, who's the cuckold now? Master Brook, Falstaff is a rogue, a cuckolded rogue. Here are his horns, Master Brook. And, Master Brook, he has enjoyed nothing of Ford's except his laundry basket, his club and twenty pounds of money, which must be paid back to Master Brook. His horses have been seized for it, Master Brook.
Sir John, we have had ill luck, we could never meet. I will never take / you for my love again, but I will always count you my deer.
Sir John, we've had bad luck; we could never meet. I'll never take you as my love again, but I'll always count you my dear deer.
I do begin to perceive that I am made an ass.
I'm beginning to see that I've been made an ass of.
Ay, and an ox too. Both the proofs are extant.
Yes, and an ox too. Both proofs are on your head.

And these are not fairies? I was three or four times in the thought / they were not fairies; and yet the guiltiness of my mind, the sudden / surprise of my powers, drove the grossness of the foppery into a / received belief, in despite of the teeth of all rhyme and reason, that / they were fairies. See now how wit may be made a Jack-a-Lent when 'tis / upon ill employment!

And these aren't fairies? Three or four times I thought they weren't fairies; and yet my guilty conscience and the sudden shock to my senses turned this crude trickery into a firm belief, against all rhyme and reason, that they were fairies. See now how wit can be made a puppet when it's put to bad use!
Sir John Falstaff, serve Got, and leave your desires, and fairies will / not pinse you.
Sir John Falstaff, serve God and give up your desires, and fairies won't pinch you.
And leave you your jealousies too, I pray you.
And you give up your jealousy too, please.
I will never mistrust my wife again, till thou art able to woo her in / good English.
I'll never mistrust my wife again until you're able to woo her in good English.

Have I laid my brain in the sun, and dried it, that it wants matter to / prevent so gross o'erreaching as this? Am I ridden with a Welsh goat / too? Shall I have a cox-comb of frieze? 'Tis time I were choked with a / piece of toasted cheese.

Have I left my brain out in the sun and dried it out, so that it lacks the sense to avoid such a crude trick as this? Am I made a fool of by a Welsh goat as well? Shall I wear a fool's cap made of Welsh wool? It's time I choked on a piece of toasted cheese.
Seese is not good to give putter. Your belly is all putter.
Cheese is not good to give with butter. Your belly is all butter.
"Seese" and "putter"? Have I lived to stand at the taunt of one that / makes fritters of English? This is enough to be the decay of lust and / late-walking through the realm.
"Seese" and "putter"? Have I lived to be mocked by someone who makes fritters of English? This is enough to ruin lust and late-night prowling throughout the kingdom.

Why, Sir John, do you think, though we would have thrust virtue out of / our hearts by the head and shoulders, and have given ourselves without / scruple to hell, that ever the devil could have made you our delight?
Why, Sir John, do you think that even if we had thrown virtue out of our hearts by the head and shoulders and given ourselves to hell without a qualm, the devil could ever have made you our delight?
What, a hodge-pudding? A bag of flax?
What, a stuffed sausage? A sack of flax?
Old, cold, withered, and of intolerable entrails?
Old, cold, withered and with unbearable guts?
And one that is as slanderous as Satan?
And as wicked as his wife?
And as wicked as Job's wife?
And given to fornications, and to taverns, and sack, and wine, and / metheglins, and to drinkings and swearings and starings, pribbles and / prabbles?
And given to fornication, and to taverns, and sack, and wine, and mead, and to drinking and swearing and staring, squabbling and quarrelling?
Well, I am your theme. You have the start of me. I am dejected, I am / not able to answer the Welsh flannel. Ignorance itself is a plummet / o'er me. Use me as you will.
Well, I'm your subject. You have the advantage of me. I'm downcast; I'm not able to answer this Welsh flannel. Ignorance itself has sunk me. Do what you like with me.

Marry, sir, we'll bring you to Windsor to one Master Brook, that you / have cozened of money, to whom you should have been a pander. Over and / above that you have suffered, I think to repay that money will be a / biting affliction.

Well, sir, we'll take you to Windsor to a certain Master Brook, whom you have swindled out of money and for whom you were going to be a pimp. On top of everything you have suffered, I think paying back that money will be a painful torment.
Yet be cheerful, knight. Thou shalt eat a posset tonight at my house, / where I will desire thee to laugh at my wife, that now laughs at thee. / Tell her Master Slender hath married her daughter.
But cheer up, knight. You'll have a hot spiced drink at my house tonight, where I'll ask you to laugh at my wife, who is laughing at you now. Tell her Master Slender has married her daughter.
[Aside] Doctors doubt that. If Anne Page be my daughter, she is, by / this, Doctor Caius' wife.
(Aside) Doctors doubt that. If Anne Page is my daughter, she's Doctor Caius's wife by now.
Son, how now! How now, son, have you dispatched?
Son, what news? What news, son, have you done it?
Dispatched? I'll make the best in Gloucestershire know on't. Would I / were hanged, la, else!
Done it? I'll make the greatest men in Gloucestershire hear about it. Or else may I be hanged, I swear!

I came yonder at Eton to marry Mistress Anne Page, and she's a great / lubberly boy. If it had not been i' the church, I would have swinged / him, or he should have swinged me. If I did not think it had been Anne / Page, would I might never stir! And 'tis a postmaster's boy.

I went over to Eton to marry Mistress Anne Page, and she's a great clumsy boy. If we hadn't been in church, I'd have thrashed him, or he would have thrashed me. If I didn't think it was Anne Page, may I never move again! And it's the postmaster's boy.
Upon my life, then, you took the wrong.
On my life, then, you took the wrong one.
What need you tell me that? I think so, when I took a boy for a girl. / If I had been married to him, for all he was in woman's apparel, I / would not have had him.
Why do you need to tell me that? I think so too, when I took a boy for a girl. If I had married him, even though he was dressed as a woman, I wouldn't have had him.
Why, this is your own folly. Did not I tell you how you should know my / daughter by her garments?
Why, this is your own stupidity. Didn't I tell you how you would recognise my daughter by her clothes?
I went to her in white and cried "mum", and she cried "budget", as Anne / and I had appointed, and yet it was not Anne, but a postmaster's boy.
I went to her in white and said "mum", and she said "budget", as Anne and I had arranged; and yet it wasn't Anne but a postmaster's boy.
Good George, be not angry. I knew of your purpose, turned my daughter / into green, and indeed she is now with the doctor at the deanery, and / there married.
Good George, don't be angry. I knew of your plan and dressed my daughter in green instead, and in fact she's now with the doctor at the deanery, and married there.
Vere is Mistress Page? By gar, I am cozened, I ha' married un garçon, / a boy; un paysan, by gar, a boy. It is not Anne Page. By gar, I am / cozened.
Where is Mistress Page? By God, I've been swindled; I have married a boy, a peasant, by God, a boy. It is not Anne Page. By God, I've been swindled.
Why, did you take her in green?
Why, did you take the one in green?
Ay, by gar, and 'tis a boy. By gar, I'll raise all Windsor.
Yes, by God, and it's a boy. By God, I'll raise all of Windsor.
This is strange. Who hath got the right Anne?
This is strange. Who has got the real Anne?
My heart misgives me. Here comes Master Fenton.—How now, Master Fenton!
I have a bad feeling about this. Here comes Master Fenton. Well, Master Fenton!
Pardon, good father. Good my mother, pardon.
Forgive me, good father. My good mother, forgive me.
Now, mistress, how chance you went not with Master Slender?
Now, young lady, how is it you didn't go with Master Slender?
Why went you not with Master Doctor, maid?
Why didn't you go with the Doctor, girl?

You do amaze her. Hear the truth of it. / You would have married her most shamefully, / Where there was no proportion held in love. / The truth is, she and I, long since contracted, / Are now so sure that nothing can dissolve us. / Th' offence is holy that she hath committed, / And this deceit loses the name of craft, / Of disobedience, or unduteous title, / Since therein she doth evitate and shun / A thousand irreligious cursed hours, / Which forced marriage would have brought upon her.

You are bewildering her. Hear the truth of it. You would have married her most shamefully, to men she could never match in love. The truth is that she and I, engaged long ago, are now so firmly bound that nothing can separate us. The offence she has committed is a holy one, and this deceit no longer deserves to be called cunning, disobedience or lack of duty, since by it she avoids and escapes a thousand unholy, cursed hours that a forced marriage would have brought her.
Stand not amazed, here is no remedy. / In love, the heavens themselves do guide the state. / Money buys lands, and wives are sold by fate.
Don't stand there amazed; there's nothing to be done. In love, the heavens themselves decide what happens. Money buys land, but wives are given out by fate.
I am glad, though you have ta'en a special stand to strike at me, that / your arrow hath glanced.
I'm glad that, though you took careful aim at me, your arrow has glanced off and hit you too.
Well, what remedy? Fenton, heaven give thee joy! / What cannot be eschewed must be embraced.
Well, what can be done? Fenton, heaven give you joy! What can't be avoided must be welcomed.
When night-dogs run, all sorts of deer are chased.
When dogs run at night, all kinds of deer get hunted.
Well, I will muse no further.—Master Fenton, / Heaven give you many, many merry days! / Good husband, let us every one go home, / And laugh this sport o'er by a country fire, / Sir John and all.
Well, I won't brood about it any more. Master Fenton, heaven give you many, many happy days! Good husband, let's all go home and laugh this game over by a country fire, Sir John and all.
Let it be so, Sir John, / To Master Brook you yet shall hold your word, / For he tonight shall lie with Mistress Ford.
So be it. Sir John, you'll still keep your word to Master Brook, because tonight he'll sleep with Mistress Ford.
